item.title: Four months after Rafael, the reviews are under way. A pastor and a deckhand say what they'd ask
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman, Sam Delacroix
item.description: Water, aid equity, port security and contracting are all under review. Two people who lived through the storm's hardest moments say what reviewers should hear.
item.content:encoded:
The fellowship hall smells like coffee and bleach on a Tuesday morning in January. Pastor Gloria Whitfield is sorting donated blankets into piles by size, the same way she sorted cases of water in September.

Four months after Hurricane Rafael, rebuilding continues across the Coastal Bend, and reviews of water, aid equity, port security and contracting are under way. Some have already produced news. The city plans to harden the water plant's power feeds. The Coast Guard and a federal cyber agency issued an advisory on vendor access to cargo systems. The Navy put its Texas air stations under a security review.

For Whitfield, the review that matters most is about who got help. Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods like hers received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, according to a December analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher. The county and FEMA have promised door-to-door registration there. Last week, a federal civil forfeiture filing said about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid went to accounts tied to two storm contractors; its claims have not been proven in court.

"I want the reviewers to come sit in this hall for one morning," Whitfield said. "Not to take a picture. To answer the door when somebody knocks with a problem. Then write the report."

Down the coast, Eddie Fontenot has a different question. The 29-year-old deckhand broke his arm and suffered a concussion when an explosive device went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28. Last week, U.S. officials said a foreign government, which they did not name, was behind both the channel devices and an intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems.

"I'm grateful I'm here. Grateful for the guys who got me out," Fontenot said. "But I want somebody to tell me how they keep it from happening to the next guy. That's my whole question."

His arm is out of the cast, and he said he has been cleared to go back to work. "Yeah. I'm going back," he said. "It's what I do."

Whitfield said four months is too soon for anyone to call the job finished. "Ask me again at a year," she said. "Ask me again at two."

item.title: In the neighborhoods that got the least, news of $3.9 million in diverted aid lands hard
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid at about half their share of residents. Now a federal filing says millions in disaster aid were diverted to accounts tied to two storm contractors.
item.content:encoded:
Pastor Gloria Whitfield read the news on her phone in the fellowship hall Thursday afternoon, between a delivery of diapers and a call about a leaking roof. Then she read it again, out loud, to nobody in particular.

A federal civil forfeiture filing says bank accounts tied to two companies hired after Hurricane Rafael, Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. According to the filing, an offshore company, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, owns both firms. A civil forfeiture case is brought against money, not people; it is not a criminal charge, and its claims have not been proven in court.

"Three point nine million dollars," Whitfield said. "I have families on my list who got nothing, or half of nothing. And the filing says disaster money ended up in accounts tied to contractors? Lord, give me patience, because I am all out."

Whitfield's neighborhood is one of the low-income surge-zone neighborhoods that, according to a December analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher Dr. Sofia Marquez, received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. Her church hub was handing out food and water before official distribution arrived after the storm. In mid-December, the county and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in those neighborhoods.

Marquez cautioned against blending the two stories. "These are separate problems, and it matters not to blur them," she said. "The gap we measured is about who got reached in the first place. Diverted aid, as the filing describes it, is about where money went. But for a family, both end the same way: the help doesn't arrive."

Marquez said her team plans to keep tracking aid by tract once door-to-door registration gets under way. "If outreach works, the numbers should move. If they don't move, that tells you something too," she said.

Separately, FEMA said in November that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over and that affected applicants would be repaid.

Whitfield said she would keep doing what she has done since September, and she wants the door-to-door teams to start soon.

"The money can sort itself out in court," she said. "The roof on the next block can't wait for a judge."

item.title: What Tuesday's attribution says, and what it leaves out
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Officials blamed a foreign government they did not name for the tanker intrusion and the channel devices. Here is what was said, what wasn't, and what comes next.
item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday morning, ships moved past the Port Aransas jetties the way they have since mid-November, through water that Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams spent two weeks searching this fall. The question hanging over that water now has part of an answer.

On Tuesday, U.S. officials attributed two things to a foreign government they did not name: the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems as Hurricane Rafael arrived in September, and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. They called both attempts to exploit the hurricane.

The intrusion is the one the Coast Guard first described six days after landfall, when it said investigators were looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. The tankers released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at an Inner Harbor berth. There were two devices: one that exploded beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties Oct. 28, injuring two crew members, and a second that Navy teams found near the entrance channel and rendered safe in early November.

What officials did not say is just as important. They did not name the government, describe their evidence or say whether anyone will be charged, and they did not tie the attribution to any other event.

"We can confirm the investigation is continuing. We have no further comment," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division.

An attribution is a government's public judgment about who is responsible. It is not a court case, and the evidence behind it is often kept out of public view.

For the companies that run ships and terminals, the practical advice has not changed, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. "Who did it matters to investigators. For an operator, the job is the same either way: know every vendor that can reach your cargo systems remotely, and be able to cut them off fast," she said. Last week, the Coast Guard and CISA issued an advisory urging vessel operators to review that access.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman, said the teams that swept the channel did their work long before Tuesday. "The channel was cleared in November, and it's open," she said. "Who put the devices there is a question for investigators. Keeping the water safe is ours."

For the tug crews, line handlers and pilots who lost two weeks of work in the fall, Tuesday's announcement answers what happened more than who did it. Coastline Public Radio will report what officials release as the investigation continues.

item.title: Hardening the water plant: why the power feeds, and what the parts delay taught a supplier
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: The city's plan targets the power feeds that failed at landfall. The pump-parts supplier whose warehouse flooded says resilience is also about where spare parts sit.
item.content:encoded:
On a cold Monday morning in Calallen, the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant hums along the Nueces River as if September never happened. The city's plan, announced Sunday, is meant to make sure the next storm doesn't silence it.

The plan is to harden the plant's power feeds. When Hurricane Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, both feeds failed early in the storm, pumps were damaged and water pressure dropped across the city. A citywide boil-water notice lasted from Sept. 18 to Oct. 23.

"Hardening the feeds comes first, because without power nothing else at that plant matters," said Teresa Gallegos, the water utility's spokeswoman.

Power was only part of the delay. After the storm, the utility said damaged pumps needed replacement parts and temporary pumps limited capacity. Then the parts were held up: the supplier's local warehouse had flooded, and the parts had to ship from out of state. They arrived Oct. 20.

Sandra Ybarra, sales manager at Delta Pumps & Controls, the supplier, said she has spent the fall thinking about where parts sit. "We had the right parts. They were in the wrong building, under water," Ybarra said. "After that, you look at a map differently. A spare that floods with the thing it's supposed to fix isn't really a spare."

She said the company is looking at keeping critical stock farther inland. "I'm still sorry about those weeks. People were boiling water and I was on the phone with freight companies," she said. "Next time I want the part on a truck before the storm makes landfall."

The city has not described which methods it will use to harden the feeds. Utilities elsewhere have buried lines, raised equipment above flood levels and added independent sources of power, but each approach comes with its own cost and timeline.

For Calallen residents, who lived closest to the plant through the five weeks of the notice, the details will matter. Gallegos said the utility will share more as the plan develops.

"We heard people loud and clear in September and October," she said. "They want to know what we're doing and when. That's fair."

item.title: What is vendor remote access, and why are federal agencies worried about it?
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: A new Coast Guard and CISA advisory asks vessel operators to check who can reach their cargo systems from outside the ship. Here is what that means in plain terms.
item.content:encoded:
When oil spread across Nueces Bay in September, most people on shore were thinking about the hurricane. Three months later, a federal advisory asks vessel operators a quieter question: who outside the ship can reach its cargo controls?

On Tuesday, the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, known as CISA, urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. Here is what that phrase means.

Cargo systems. On a tanker, cargo-control systems run the pumps and valves that move oil into and out of the tanks. Modern systems are networked, so crews can monitor and adjust them from a control station instead of walking the deck to every valve.

Vendor remote access. The companies that build and maintain those systems often service them from a distance, logging in over a network connection to diagnose problems or update software. That saves a technician a trip to the ship. It also means a set of login credentials, somewhere on land, can reach equipment on board.

"Think of it as a spare key you gave the plumber," said Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab. "It's convenient until somebody copies it. Attackers like vendor access because it's trusted. Nobody gets alarmed when the maintenance company logs in."

Why Corpus Christi is part of the story. In September, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of the two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor spill. Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains such systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and revoked all remote access. Investigators have not announced a finding.

What operators can do. "The fix isn't exotic," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Know which vendors have access. Turn it off when it isn't needed. Watch the logs, and have someone actually read them."

Feld said she would not guess who was behind the misuse in Corpus Christi. "That's for investigators to say, and they haven't said it," she said. "What I can say is the lesson doesn't depend on the answer. Every operator should know who holds a key."

For people who live along the bays, the advisory is a reminder that the spill was not only a story about weather.

item.title: Inside the 911 gap: researchers say the next step is finding where the time went
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Median 911 response times in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods were 2.1 times those in high-income areas. The researcher behind the numbers says the data shows the size of the gap, not the reason.
item.content:encoded:
In the first days after Hurricane Rafael, the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center was taking about 2,900 calls a day, nearly ten times normal. Most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

Three months later, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher Dr. Sofia Marquez found the median 911 response time in low-income neighborhoods inside the surge zone was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. The same neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

The analysis measures how long help took. It does not, by itself, explain why.

"The data gives you the size of the gap. It doesn't hand you the reason," Marquez said. "Before anyone claims to have fixed this, somebody has to trace those calls and find out where the time went. That's the work a real review does."

Some background is already on the record. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service left many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and they pushed for more evacuation rides. Under the mandatory evacuation, households without cars had to wait for the county's buses. After the storm, residents in those neighborhoods said they waited days for help. Marquez cautioned against treating any one of those facts as the explanation.

She does have recommendations. "Next time, response times should be tracked by neighborhood while the storm is happening, not three months later," she said. "If you can see the gap in real time, you can send people to close it. And aid outreach should start in the places with the fewest cars and the fewest phones, not end there."

The analysis compared census tracts: low-income neighborhoods inside the surge zone against the county's high-income areas. "We compared like with like as far as the data allows," Marquez said. "Every number in it can be checked, and I'd welcome people checking it."

Last week, Nueces County and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods.

"Numbers like that don't sit on a shelf," said Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Going door to door is one step. People in those neighborhoods are going to hold us to the rest, and they should."

Coastline Public Radio's tract-level maps are available on our website.

item.title: Navy orders security review at Texas air stations, citing drone reports and channel attack
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The review covers the Navy's air stations in Texas, including NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville. The Navy cited drone reports after Hurricane Rafael and the explosive device that closed the ship channel.
item.content:encoded:
The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, including Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville, citing drone reports after Hurricane Rafael and the attack in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel this fall.

The review was announced Sunday. Navy public affairs officers said they would not discuss security measures at the stations.

"We're not going to get into specific security measures, and I'd ask people to understand why," said Lt. Marcus Hale, public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "What I can tell you is the station is operating, and a review like this is what you do after a season like the one we just had."

The drone reports date to the first nights after the storm. Two days after Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, residents near the air station began posting videos of lights hovering over it at night. The station said it was aware of the reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations, and the FBI confirmed it was investigating. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.

The channel attack came Oct. 28, when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties, injuring two crew members. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, working with the Coast Guard, found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance channel Nov. 5. After a 14-day closure and a full sweep, the channel reopened Nov. 11. The FBI is investigating.

"The safety of the channel and the people who work on it comes first," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Our teams finished a full sweep before that channel reopened. A review asks what we learned and what we do with it."

No one has publicly been identified as responsible for the drone flights or the devices.

NAS Kingsville, southwest of Corpus Christi, trains Navy jet pilots. Like NAS Corpus Christi, it flew its training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm. Hale said families at both stations should watch official station channels for any updates.

item.title: At the Army depot, a year-end exhale after a season of leaks and long shifts
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Corpus Christi Army Depot workers came back to soaked hangars after Rafael and had the shops at full production by Halloween. As the holiday break starts, the depot says its workforce carried it.
item.content:encoded:
The parking lots at Corpus Christi Army Depot thin out a little more each afternoon this week as civilian mechanics start their holiday leave. Three months ago, many of those same workers were at home waiting for a phone call while crews assessed hangar roofs that Hurricane Rafael had torn open and soaked.

The depot, the military's main repair shop for helicopters, sits on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. Before the storm it halted work and secured helicopters and components inside its hangars. Three days after landfall, it reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion and told workers to stand by.

By the end of October, the depot said it was back at full production, with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi, the Defense Logistics Agency warehouse that supplies its shops.

"Our people came back to hangars with tarps on the roofs and water on the floors, and they went to work," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "This workforce is the mission. Nobody here forgot that, even with their own houses torn up."

The storm landed in the middle of what had been an ordinary year at the depot. In July, it was hiring helicopter mechanics, and the air station's training squadrons were on a normal summer schedule. By September, the squadrons' aircraft had flown to Fort Worth to ride out the storm; they began returning six days after landfall.

The rest of the fall brought more surprises around the station. In October, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the cause remains under review.

Kowalczyk said the depot's message to employees heading into the break was simple. "Rest. Hug your kids. Fix the fence you've been ignoring since September," she said. "We'll see you in January."

For many families in Flour Bluff and around the station, the holiday is the first real pause since the storm. The work on their own houses, Kowalczyk said, doesn't stop for leave. "A lot of folks are spending their vacation hanging drywall," she said. "That's this town. You fix the hangar, then you go home and fix the house."

item.title: Door-to-door aid registration is coming. Researchers and neighbors say it's a start.
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: County and FEMA officials will send registration teams into low-income surge-zone neighborhoods, two days after Coastline's analysis found those neighborhoods got about half their share of aid.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez of Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi found that low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. On Tuesday, Marquez said the first fix should be going door to door. On Wednesday, county and FEMA officials announced teams would do exactly that.

Marquez was careful not to claim credit. "Lots of people have been saying this for months, starting with the neighbors themselves," she said. "It's the right first step. The test is whether it reaches the people who aren't on anybody's list. The renter in the back unit. The grandmother without a phone. If the teams find them, the number moves."

The door-to-door registration will focus on low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone, the same areas where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm and where many households don't have a car.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm, said she was ready to help the teams find people.

"My door's open, and my list is long," Whitfield said. "I know who's sick, who's alone, who's scared of anybody with a clipboard. Let me walk with them the first day, and people will open up."

Marquez said she hopes the effort is measured, not just announced. "Count the doors, count the applications, count the dollars, by neighborhood," she said. "Then show us. If it works, we'll know. If it doesn't, we'll know that too."

For neighbors wary of strangers at the door, FEMA says its staff carry federal photo ID and never charge a fee. Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 and remains open online, by phone and at recovery centers for anyone who has not yet applied.

Marquez said the 911 findings deserve their own response. The median 911 response time in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. "Door-to-door helps with aid," she said. "It doesn't answer why help took more than twice as long to arrive in the first place. That's a conversation for before the next storm."

item.title: Researcher behind the aid-gap analysis lays out fixes: knock on doors, follow the bus lines
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Dr. Sofia Marquez says the gap in Hurricane Rafael aid can be narrowed, starting with how agencies reach people who can't come to them.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Sofia Marquez has spent years studying who gets help after disasters. A day after releasing her analysis of Hurricane Rafael aid, she wanted to talk about what comes next.

"I don't want this number framed and hung on a wall," said Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "I want it to change how the next dollar moves."

The analysis, by Marquez and Coastline Public Radio, found low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

Marquez laid out five recommendations drawn from her research.

Go door to door. "If the people who need help most can't get to a recovery center, the recovery center has to get to them," she said. Registration teams in the hardest-hit neighborhoods, with paper and phone options for people without internet, would reach households that online systems miss.

Follow the bus lines. Recovery centers and pop-up registration sites should sit on bus routes and near the churches and neighborhood hubs residents already trust. After the storm, those hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets.

Make help human and multilingual. "A form in English on a website is not access," Marquez said. She said trained neighbors, church volunteers and community health workers who speak the neighborhood's languages are often trusted more than a stranger with a clipboard.

Plan before the next storm. Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and advocates pushed for more evacuation rides. Marquez said those lists could do double duty after a storm, showing responders which households may need a knock rather than a link.

Measure as you go. "We did this analysis three months after landfall," she said. "Agencies can track who's applying and who's getting paid, by neighborhood, every week. Then you fix the gap in December instead of reading about it in March."

Marquez said none of the recommendations require new technology. "It's shoe leather," she said. "It's the oldest tool we have."

Registration for FEMA individual assistance opened Nov. 13 and remains open.

item.title: 'They Came With Pamphlets': How Disaster Fraud Targeted Corpus Christi's Most Vulnerable Neighborhoods
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: In the weeks after Hurricane Rafael, claim runners fanned out through storm-damaged Districts 3 and 4 with promises of help — and left real victims with compromised identities and pending FEMA applications they cannot explain.
item.content:encoded:
In the weeks after Hurricane Rafael, as federal Individual Assistance still had not been approved, Veronica Limas says a woman came to her door on Lipan Street with a clipboard and a stack of glossy pamphlets. The pamphlet, printed in both English and Spanish, promised to help storm victims navigate the FEMA application process. It listed a phone number and a small logo — a wave graphic — but no company name that Limas, 54, could locate or verify. She gave the woman her name, her address, photos of the two feet of water that had flooded her District 3 home, and her Social Security number. She was told help was coming. She never heard from the woman again.

Limas learned Monday, when federal prosecutors unsealed a criminal complaint naming Landmark Pacific Holdings LLC, that the visit to her door was likely not an act of charity. According to the FBI, Landmark Pacific used exactly this method — door-to-door recruiters, bilingual pamphlets, promises of FEMA assistance navigation — to collect the personal information of real storm victims in Districts 3 and 4 and then file fraudulent claims in their names. The scheme generated 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications and 187 fraudulent insurance claims totaling more than $23 million, prosecutors say. Fourteen people were arrested Monday.

The targeting of Districts 3 and 4 was not coincidental, said legal-aid workers who have been fielding calls since the arrests were announced. Those are the neighborhoods where the surge was worst, the boil-water notice lasted longest, and the 57-day wait for FEMA Individual Assistance was most financially devastating. 'These neighborhoods were already failed by the system in multiple ways,' said Adriana Flores, a staff attorney with Coastal Bend Legal Aid. 'The power stayed out longest here. The boil-water notice lasted longest here. FEMA came last here. And into that gap came people who made promises and took information.'

Flores said her office is tracking at least 34 potential victims who provided information to Landmark Pacific representatives and may now face complications with their own legitimate FEMA claims because of identity overlap in the federal database. For some, money they were legally owed has not arrived because their application is flagged for review. For others, the experience has made them reluctant to engage with official channels at all.

Limas said she plans to visit the FEMA Disaster Recovery Center on Ayers Street this week. As of Monday evening, her FEMA application remained in a 'pending verification' status she had been unable to resolve by phone. 'I did everything right,' she said. 'Or I thought I did. And now I'm the one who has to prove it.'

item.title: How we measured the aid gap: a guide to Coastline's analysis with Texas A&M-Corpus Christi
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: What "half their share" means, why the analysis uses medians for 911 response times, and what the numbers can and can't tell you.
item.content:encoded:
Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez of Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi found that low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. Here is how to read those numbers.

Which neighborhoods were compared? The analysis compared two groups of census tracts. The first is the lowest-income tracts inside the storm surge or flood zone, which also have some of the highest shares of households without a vehicle. The second is the highest-income tracts in Nueces County.

What does "half their share" mean? If aid dollars were distributed in proportion to population, each group would receive a share of aid equal to its share of residents. The low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received about half of that.

Why measure by residents and not by damage? "Per resident is the simplest fairness test. It isn't the only one," Marquez said. "Comparing aid to damage is worth doing too, and we'd welcome anyone who wants to try it with us."

What is a median 911 response time? The median is the middle value: half of responses were faster, half slower. Medians aren't thrown off by a handful of extreme cases. A median 2.1 times as long means the typical call in those neighborhoods waited a little more than twice as long for a response as the typical call in high-income areas.

What can't the analysis tell you? It shows where the gap is, not every cause. "Factors worth examining include road and bridge closures during and after the storm, vehicle access, internet access and how people learned about aid," Marquez said. After the storm, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway stayed closed until inspections were finished Sept. 17, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown.

Does it say anyone acted wrongly? No. It measures outcomes. Explaining them, and deciding what to change, comes next.

What data was used? Census demographics, 911 response records and aid payment totals, each analyzed by census tract.

Have a question we didn't answer? Send it to the Coastline newsroom, and we'll add answers to this guide.

item.title: Half their share: low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got less storm aid and waited longer for 911, analysis finds
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: An analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher finds low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
item.content:encoded:
In the days after Hurricane Rafael came ashore, the 911 center serving Corpus Christi and Nueces County took about 2,900 calls a day at the peak, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Three months later, an analysis shows how those neighborhoods fared once help started moving.

Low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, according to an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. The median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

"Half. Not a little less. Half," Marquez said. "These are the neighborhoods with the fewest cars, the least flexible jobs and often the least reliable internet. When getting help depends on getting somewhere or getting online, this is the pattern you'd expect, and it's the pattern we found."

The analysis compared groups of census tracts: the lowest-income tracts inside the surge or flood zone, where many households have no vehicle, and the highest-income tracts in Nueces County. It measured each group's share of aid dollars against its share of residents and compared typical 911 response times.

The findings put numbers on what residents and advocates described all year. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps left many households without cars in neighborhoods near the bay. When the order to leave came, those without cars depended on county buses and waited for them. After landfall, residents of low-income neighborhoods reported waiting days for help, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets. In late October, emergency room visits there were still about 40% above normal while the rest of the region was back near normal.

"We told anybody who would listen," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm. "Now it's got a number on it. I hope the number does what my voice couldn't."

Marquez cautioned that the analysis shows where the gap is, not every reason for it. "This tells you who got less, not why in every case," she said. "That's the next question, and it's answerable."

Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 and remains open.

item.title: On a feast day, a toy table: families near the bay make room for the holidays
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: As parishes marked the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Sunday, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's relief hub opened a toy table for families still recovering from Hurricane Rafael.
item.content:encoded:
Before dawn Sunday, las mañanitas drifted from a parish down the street, where families gathered with roses for the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe. By 9 a.m., a different line had formed outside Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall.

Inside, donated toys sat sorted by age on the same folding tables that held turkeys at Thanksgiving and water jugs in September. Parents picked one gift for each child and wrapped it at a table in the back, where volunteers had paper, tape and strong opinions about bows.

"Nobody's kid should have to learn about hurricanes and Santa Claus in the same year and decide Santa's the one who isn't real," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from the hall since the first days after the storm.

Rosa Elizondo came with a list for her three children and left with two of the three items checked off. "Este año, Santa viene en autobús," she said: This year, Santa comes by bus. Elizondo doesn't have a car. Neither do many of her neighbors, a gap advocates raised long before the storm.

Nearly three months after Hurricane Rafael, the hall remains a lifeline for the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm. Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13, and volunteers here have helped neighbors without smartphones fill out applications and, after FEMA said 410 applicant accounts were taken over using stolen passwords, check their deposit details.

Elizondo said her application is still pending. "I check the bank every morning. Every morning it's the same," she said. "Same is good. Same means nobody took it."

Among the volunteers carrying boxes in from a pickup were a few young sailors from the air station, there on their own time and in civilian clothes. One of them spent twenty minutes helping a grandmother choose between two dolls.

Volunteers also kept a table of donated coats and blankets by the door, a reminder that many families near the bay are still living in homes with storm damage as the nights get colder.

Whitfield said she is already thinking past Christmas.

"December, everybody remembers you," she said. "January is when the donations stop and the bills come. Remember us in January."

item.title: Damp walls and cold fronts: renters in storm-hit homes head into winter
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, renters still waiting on repairs are bracing for colder nights. A health district epidemiologist offers advice for damp, drafty homes.
item.content:encoded:
When the first real cold front of the season blew through Corpus Christi, Rosa Elizondo pulled every blanket in the duplex onto one bed and put her three children in it.

"The heater works. The window doesn't close all the way since the storm," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rents near the bay. "So we have a heater that heats the street."

Nearly three months after Hurricane Rafael, Elizondo is still waiting on her landlord to fix the window and the water-stained ceiling, and on a FEMA application she filed the week registration opened Nov. 13. She is not alone. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and in late October, health officials said emergency room visits there were still about 40% above normal, even as the rest of the region had returned to near normal.

Renters face a particular bind. They can't make major repairs themselves, and many can't afford to move. In neighborhoods where many households have no car, even getting to a hardware store or a recovery center can take half a day by bus.

Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District, offered general advice for damp, drafty homes.

"If you see or smell mold, clean small areas with soap and water and let in fresh air when you can," Shah said. "If anyone in the home has asthma or another breathing problem, call your doctor sooner rather than later. And please, never heat your home with a gas stove, an oven or a grill. Carbon monoxide doesn't smell like anything."

Shah said people with lingering health concerns after the storm should not wait for a crisis. "If you've been coughing for weeks or your child's asthma is getting worse, that's a reason to be seen," she said.

Elizondo said she has learned to improvise. She tapes plastic over the window at night and takes it down in the morning, so the landlord can see the damage if he ever comes by.

"Mis hijos think it's camping. Indoor camping," she said. "I let them think it. Camping is free."

item.title: Five weeks after the jetty blast, a tug deckhand counts the days until he can go back out
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Eddie Fontenot was one of two crew members hurt when an explosive device detonated beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay. He and his captain talk about recovery, routine and the channel they work.
item.content:encoded:
Eddie Fontenot flexes the fingers of the arm that spent most of November in a cast. They work. He seems a little surprised.

"Arm's good. Head's mostly good," said Fontenot, 29, a deckhand for Laguna Towing. "I sleep with the TV on now. That's new."

Fontenot was one of two crew members injured around 1 a.m. Oct. 28, when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties. He suffered a broken arm and a concussion. The blast damaged the tug, and the Coast Guard closed the ship channel.

Two days later, the Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the channel with the Coast Guard, and on Nov. 5 they found a second device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe. The channel reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure and a full sweep. The FBI is investigating.

Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, has towed ships in the Corpus Christi channel for 30 years and was master of Corrin Bay that night. He said he has been back on the water since mid-November, once the company had a boat for him.

"The channel's been swept end to end by people who know what they're doing," Dupree said. "I trust them. I run it every day. My crew runs it every day."

Dupree said he gets one question more than any other: who did it. He doesn't answer it.

"I drive tugs," he said. "The FBI can do their job, and I'll do mine."

Fontenot hopes to be cleared to go back to work after the new year. He said he misses the routine more than the paycheck, though he misses the paycheck, too.

"People think I'd be scared to go back out," he said. "I'm more scared of sitting on my couch until March."

Dupree said there is a spot on his crew whenever the doctor signs off. "He's a good hand," Dupree said. "He was a good hand that night, too. First thing he asked was whether everybody else was OK."

For now, Fontenot is spending the holidays with family and going to physical therapy. He has one goal for Christmas.

"Sleep through the night," he said. "With the TV off."

item.title: Why the new rumor wave about "stolen aid" spreads, and how to sort real questions from false claims
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Posts claiming contractors are stealing hurricane aid mix legitimate questions with invented details. A threat researcher explains why that mix travels fast in neighborhoods still waiting for help.
item.content:encoded:
The posts land between photos of curbside debris piles and requests for a working dryer. Contractors are stealing your aid, they say, and nobody will tell you.

It is the second big rumor wave since Hurricane Rafael. In the first days after landfall, viral posts falsely claimed the military was seizing homes and that aid would go only to wealthy neighborhoods. This one, which picked up over the Thanksgiving weekend, is about contracts.

Fact-checkers say some of the questions are legitimate and some of the specific posts are false. The county's $14.2 million emergency debris contract went to Vantorra Restoration without competitive bidding, a fair subject for scrutiny. On Sunday, the Navy suspended the air station's emergency fuel supplier, Quellmar Fuel Partners, pending a fuel quality review; the company says its fuel meets specifications. But posts claiming the debris contract was worth $140 million, or that FEMA stopped paying families to pay contractors, are false, Harborline 6 found.

Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab who studies influence campaigns, said the mix is the point.

"The most effective false stories are built around something true," Feld said. "A real contract, a real delay, real anger. Then somebody adds a number that isn't real, and the true part carries the false part along with it."

The posts land hardest where people are still waiting. Residents in low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and many are still waiting on aid applications filed since registration opened Nov. 13.

"When people are waiting, any story that explains the wait feels true," Feld said. "That's not a character flaw. That's being human in a bad month."

Feld offered a short checklist. Find the document behind the claim. Check any number against public records. Notice when a post leans on all-caps outrage instead of evidence. And ask whether the post wants you to click, donate or share before you've had time to think.

Asked who is behind the new posts, Feld declined to say. "I don't do attribution by vibes," she said.

Questions about a specific contract can go to the agency that awarded it. County contract records can be requested from the county, and federal contract awards are posted in public databases.

item.title: Fuel supplier disputes Navy suspension as review of air station generator failure continues
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Quellmar Fuel Partners says every delivery met specifications. The Navy says it won't get ahead of a quality review tied to October's generator failure at NAS Corpus Christi.
item.content:encoded:
On an ordinary day, a backup generator is the least interesting machine on a military installation. It sits, it gets tested, and it waits for the moment the grid goes down. At Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, that moment came in October, and the generator failed.

Now the Navy has suspended the company that supplied the station's emergency fuel after Hurricane Rafael. The station said Sunday that Quellmar Fuel Partners was suspended pending a fuel quality review linked to the generator failure. On Monday, the company pushed back.

"Every load we delivered met specifications, and we have the paperwork to show it," said Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager. "We stepped in when the station's regular supplier was flooded out. We're disappointed, and we're cooperating with the review."

Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station, said the review would run its course. "The review will determine what happened," he said. "Until it's complete, we're not going to speculate about the cause."

Some background helps explain what is at stake. Military fuel is bought to written specifications, and suppliers typically provide paperwork certifying that a delivery meets them. A quality review generally checks those records, and any samples kept, against what the contract requires. The Navy has not said what its review has examined or what, if anything, it has found.

The timeline, from public statements and records: The station's regular fuel supplier flooded in the storm. Federal contract records that became public Oct. 4 showed a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the station to Quellmar. On Oct. 25, the station said its backup generator had failed during a power interruption, that power had been restored and that the cause was under review. On Sunday, the Navy tied that review to fuel quality and suspended the supplier.

For people who live and work on the station, Hale said, the power is on. He declined to discuss backup arrangements, citing security.

Kerr said she expects the company to be cleared. "When the facts come out, they'll show we did our job," she said.

The Navy has not said how long the review will take.

item.title: Thanksgiving in the fellowship hall: a relief hub feeds a neighborhood still waiting
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hub served a holiday meal to neighbors waiting on aid, repairs and answers.
item.content:encoded:
By 10 a.m. Thursday, the line outside the fellowship hall reached the church sign and bent around the corner. Inside, volunteers in plastic gloves carved turkeys on folding tables, and a teenager with a clipboard asked every family the same question: "How many at home?"

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, has run a relief hub from this hall since the first days after Hurricane Rafael, when church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay. On Thanksgiving, the hub did what it has done all fall, only with gravy.

"People think the storm is over because the boil-water notice is over and the news moved on," Whitfield said. "Come stand at my door. The storm is over for some people. It's not over here."

The streets around the church are part of the low-lying, low-income stretch near the bay where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm. Many households here have no car, a gap advocates warned about over the summer, when they pushed for more evacuation rides. In late October, health officials said emergency room visits across the region were back near normal, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Nov. 13. Whitfield said volunteers have spent much of the past two weeks helping neighbors without smartphones fill out applications and, since FEMA's warning about unauthorized account access, check whether anyone has changed their deposit details. On Wednesday, the agency disclosed that attackers armed with passwords stolen from other sites had taken over 410 applicant accounts. It said affected applicants would be repaid.

"Half my people don't have an email address, and the other half share one with a cousin," Whitfield said. "And now we're telling them to watch out for hackers. Lord, have mercy."

By late morning the hall had run out of rolls, and a volunteer drove to the grocery store for more. Children ate pie on the steps. An older man in a Navy veteran's cap asked if he could take a plate to a neighbor who couldn't walk that far, and a volunteer made up two.

Whitfield said the hub would stay open through the holidays.

"We'll be here at Christmas, too," she said. "I'm not going anywhere, and neither are they."

item.title: For families living close to the edge, a changed deposit could mean a missed rent payment
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: FEMA has confirmed unauthorized access to some aid accounts. In neighborhoods that waited longest for help after Rafael, people say the stakes of a wrong bank number are measured in days, not dollars.
item.content:encoded:
On Saturday morning, the whiteboard in Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall had a new line at the top, written in red marker: "CHECK YOUR DEPOSIT. EVERY DAY."

On Friday, FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some disaster aid applicant accounts and asked every applicant to check their direct-deposit information. Earlier in the week, some applicants in Nueces County said they had found bank details on their applications that they had not entered. How many accounts were affected, and how they were accessed, FEMA has not said.

For a household with savings, a problem like that is a hassle. For many of the families Whitfield serves, in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, it is the difference between paying rent and not.

"If your money goes to somebody else's account, you can call and fix it, sure. How long does that take?" Whitfield said. "My people don't have a cushion. A week late is a late fee. Two weeks late is a conversation with the landlord nobody wants to have."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said applicants who find a problem should call the helpline right away. "Verify your information now, even if you checked last week," Ostrander said. "FEMA will never call, text or email you to ask for your password. If someone does, it isn't us."

These are the same neighborhoods where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm, and where emergency room visits were still running about 40% above normal in late October. Many residents registered for aid on borrowed phones and laptops at church and neighborhood hubs because they have no computer at home.

That creates a practical problem. Checking an account every day, as Whitfield's whiteboard advises, is easy with a smartphone and a data plan. It is harder for a household that shares one phone or relies on the hall's laptops.

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who registered on the first day, has been checking hers from her phone on the bus between clients. Her information has not changed. Her application is still pending while FEMA reviews the school letter she sent to prove she lives in her rental.

"First I'm waiting for the money. Now I'm guarding money I don't have yet," Elizondo said. "That's a new kind of tired."

Whitfield said the hall would keep its laptops out through Thanksgiving week. "We'll check it with you," she said. "That's what we're here for."

item.title: Rosa Elizondo registered for FEMA aid. Two days later, her application is stuck on a lease
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: A home health aide who took two buses to register Saturday learned Monday that FEMA needs more proof she lives where she lives. Her landlord doesn't answer the phone.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo checked her FEMA application on her phone on the bus Monday morning, between clients. The status had changed. It did not say approved or denied. It said FEMA needed more information.

"Proof of occupancy," Elizondo said, reading it out loud at the fellowship hall that afternoon. "I occupy. I'm occupying right now. Ask my ceiling."

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three, registered for federal individual assistance Saturday, the day registration opened in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. She took two buses to a recovery center and waited most of the morning. She brought her lease. But the lease, she said, is a one-page form her landlord wrote years ago, with no date on the second line and her name spelled wrong.

Her landlord has not returned her calls since the storm, she said, except to say repairs to the leaking hallway ceiling are coming "soon."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said renters who cannot easily prove occupancy have options. "A utility bill, a pay stub, a letter from a school or an employer with the address, a bank statement, many documents can help show where you lived," Ostrander said, speaking generally about the process. "If FEMA asks for more information, respond as soon as you can, and call the helpline if you're not sure what to send."

At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, volunteers helped Elizondo find a school letter for her youngest child that showed her address and photographed it with her phone.

"This is what it looks like," Whitfield said. "The people with the least paperwork are the people who need the help the most. Rosa did everything right, and the system still says, prove it."

Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay waited days for help after Rafael, and church and neighborhood hubs filled gaps before official aid arrived. Whitfield said she expects many renters on her list to hit the same snag.

Elizondo uploaded the school letter before her next client visit. "Now I wait again," she said. "I'm very good at waiting. I should get paid for it. Maybe that's what FEMA's for."

item.title: Aid registration is open. For some neighborhoods, the hard part is getting to it
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: FEMA says phone and online registration count the same as standing in line. A pastor whose fellowship hall became a relief hub says the gap is phones, rides and time off work.
item.content:encoded:
At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, the folding tables that held water pallets in September held something else Saturday: two borrowed laptops, a phone charger strip and a hand-lettered sign reading "FEMA help here. Bring your papers."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Saturday for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, and lines formed early at recovery centers. For residents of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, getting registered depends on things many people elsewhere take for granted: a car, a working phone, a data plan and a day off.

"Everybody on my list needs to register. Most of them can't get to a center, and plenty of those don't have a phone that will hold a charge through the hold music," said Whitfield, 59, who keeps a binder of neighbors' needs and has used it since before the storm. "So we bring the phones and the patience."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said registration by phone or online counts the same as registration in person. "There's no advantage to standing in line," she said. "We want every eligible household registered, and we'll keep saying that."

The neighborhoods where Whitfield works were among the slowest to get help after Rafael. Residents reported waiting days for assistance, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks. Last month, health officials said emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay remained about 40% above normal, after visits elsewhere had settled.

Long before the storm, transit advocates warned that bus gaps left many households near the bay without a way to evacuate. Those same gaps now shape who can reach a recovery center on a Saturday.

Whitfield said volunteers helped a steady stream of neighbors register by phone Saturday, writing registration numbers on index cards so no one would lose them. "This is the first step," she said. "I'm not going to call it a good day until the help actually shows up. But it's a step."

Coastline Public Radio will follow how aid reaches neighborhoods across the Coastal Bend in the coming months.

item.title: Hospital Report Finds Rafael's Illness Wave Hit Spanish-Speaking Households at Double the Expected Rate
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: A joint after-action analysis from Shoreline Regional and Bay City Medical centers documents 4,217 hurricane-related patients, a preventable 12-hour bilingual notification gap, and systemic failures that amplified suffering among the region's most vulnerable residents.
item.content:encoded:
When Shoreline Regional Medical Center and Bay City Medical Center released their joint Hurricane Rafael After-Action Report on Saturday, they did something most hospitals don't do after a disaster: they quantified who got sicker, and why. The 87-page document, the product of a two-month internal review, traces more than 4,200 patients directly to the storm — and reveals that Spanish-dominant households bore a disproportionate share of a preventable illness outbreak tied to contaminated water.

The two hospitals treated 4,217 hurricane-related patients between Sept. 11 and Oct. 14. Among those, 1,820 patients were treated for Cryptosporidium and Giardia infection between Sept. 29 and Oct. 12 — a cluster investigators attribute primarily to consumption of unboiled tap water in Districts 3 and 4 during the extended boil-water notice period. Among early-wave gastroenteritis admissions, 57 percent came from Spanish-dominant households, compared with those households' 36-percent share of the affected population. The 21-percentage-point gap, the report states, is 'consistent with' the documented delay of more than 12 hours before the Spanish-language version of the boil-water notice was distributed.

The report names no outlet directly, but its phrasing aligns closely with disclosures that Corpus Christi's primary Spanish-language radio station did not receive the boil-water notice from Nueces County emergency management until more than 12 hours after English-language outlets were notified. 'The timing differential in public notification corresponded to a measurable differential in illness exposure,' the report states. 'This finding should be incorporated into regional emergency communications planning.' It is the first time an institutional document has attempted to quantify the public-health cost of that delay.

The report also documents a near-catastrophic hospital generator diesel shortage five days after landfall, when both facilities were operating at or above capacity — SRMC at 140 percent of its licensed census — and commercial fuel deliveries had been suspended due to road closures. The situation was resolved when National Guard logistics personnel delivered emergency fuel that afternoon. The report recommends a minimum 10-day on-site fuel reserve for all facilities with critical-care designations, a standard currently met by fewer than a third of Texas Gulf Coast hospitals.

SRMC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Patricia Cabrera said in a statement Saturday that the hospital has already begun implementing report recommendations, including 24/7 Spanish-speaking clinical staffing in the emergency department. 'These findings are uncomfortable,' she said. 'They should be. We will not be comfortable until they cannot happen again.'

item.title: After a hurricane and a blast, Fort Hood brigade's helicopters load at Corpus Christi
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The aviation brigade's equipment is going aboard a sealift ship and will sail over the next five days. The Army describes the destination only as an overseas rotation.
item.content:encoded:
Before sunrise Friday, the first of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters, shrink-wrapped against salt air, rolled down to a berth at the Port of Corpus Christi. By first light, cranes and ramps were moving equipment aboard a sealift ship.

It was a movement the brigade expected to make in late summer.

The Army scheduled the brigade to move its helicopters and equipment through Corpus Christi for an overseas rotation. Hurricane Rafael forced a first postponement in September, and the ship channel then stayed shut for weeks after the storm. The channel partly reopened in October, but on Oct. 28 an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed it again, delaying the movement a second time. The channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep.

"Loading is under way," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Our soldiers have been ready for a long time. They've been patient, and so have their families. Today we get to do the job." The brigade's equipment will sail over the next five days, Price said. He described the destination only as an overseas rotation and declined to discuss the ship, the route or the number of aircraft.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the outload was moving alongside the commercial restart. "This port has been a strategic military seaport for a long time, and this is what that means: a day after the channel opens, we are loading a brigade and tankers at the same time," Salinas said. "Our people have been waiting for this as much as anyone."

For military watchers, the significance of the departure is the delay that preceded it. A movement planned for summer has slipped into late fall, first because of weather and then because of a closed channel. Price would not say whether the delay affected the brigade's mission. "We go when we can go," he said. "We're going now."

For families at Fort Hood, the next week will bring the familiar mix of pride and goodbye. Price said the Army would continue to share updates through public channels. On the Coastal Bend, it means the sight of olive-drab vehicles and helicopters on the docks, and then, once the ship sails, an empty berth.

item.title: FEMA approves aid for households, eight weeks after Rafael. Here's why it took this long
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Registration for Individual Assistance opens Saturday in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Officials say slowed damage assessments held up the decision.
item.content:encoded:
For eight weeks, the answer to the question asked most often in the Coastal Bend's hardest-hit neighborhoods has been the same two words: not yet. On Wednesday, the answer changed.

FEMA approved Individual Assistance for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, opening the way for federal help to households damaged by Hurricane Rafael. Registration opens Saturday, Nov. 13.

"This is the decision people have been waiting for," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Households with storm damage or losses can start registering Saturday. Use only FEMA's official website, its helpline or a disaster recovery center."

Why did it take this long? The federal disaster declaration issued four days after landfall covered debris removal and emergency protective measures, the costs local governments carry first. Help for individual households hinged on joint damage assessments by federal, state and local teams. Those dragged as teams ran into restrictions in the oiled zone, roads still under water and the sheer amount of damage. In October, the state formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance.

"Nobody in our office liked telling people to wait," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "But you can't approve help for houses nobody has been able to look at. Now we get to stop saying 'not yet.'"

The wait fell hardest on households with the least cushion. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks, and in late October health officials said emergency room visits from those neighborhoods were still about 40% above normal.

Ostrander said people can use the next three days to get ready: find a photo ID, insurance papers if they have them and pictures of the damage, and, for renters, something that shows they lived at the address. Pruitt said church and neighborhood hubs are a good place to start for anyone without a computer or a reliable phone.

Registering is free. Pruitt reminded residents that the city warned in September about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal, and said no one should register through a link that arrives by text or email.

Saturday will be the first day. For many families near the bay, it will not be the last thing they wait for.

item.title: Eight Weeks On, Federal Aid Is Approved — But For Many Corpus Christi Families, the Wait Already Cost Them
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: FEMA's Individual Assistance approval brings relief to hurricane survivors Wednesday, but advocates say the 57-day gap has left lasting financial damage — particularly for renters and Spanish-speaking households who had the fewest safety nets.
item.content:encoded:
By 8 a.m. Wednesday, a line had already formed outside the Oveal Williams Senior Center on Martin Luther King Drive, where FEMA plans to open one of its three Disaster Recovery Centers on Saturday. Word had spread that federal help was finally coming, and people came to ask when. Many of those waiting had been displaced from Districts 3 and 4, the neighborhoods hardest hit by Hurricane Rafael's storm surge and by the power outages that followed. Some carried folders stuffed with photographs, utility bills, and lease agreements — documents they had been told to gather weeks ago, in anticipation of the federal aid that was approved Wednesday.

FEMA's approval of Individual Assistance for Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties unlocks rental assistance, home repair grants, and personal property replacement for eligible storm survivors. Registration opens Saturday, Nov. 13, at DisasterAssistance.gov, by phone at 1-800-621-FEMA and at the recovery centers. But for many families, the 57-day interval between Rafael's landfall and the approval has already meant missed rent payments, maxed credit cards, and decisions to move in with relatives across the state — or to leave altogether.

'We told people to hold on, help was coming,' said Dolores Vasquez, outreach director for Nueces County Community Action, which has fielded thousands of calls from storm-affected residents since Rafael made landfall. 'But you can't hold on for eight weeks when your landlord is calling every three days. Some families are already gone.' The delay, federal officials say, stemmed partly from the prolonged collapse of the electrical grid, which prevented damage inspectors from reaching and accurately assessing thousands of properties in low-lying neighborhoods. The grid in Districts 3 and 4 did not reach 80 percent restoration until mid-October.

The approval does not remediate the gap, but advocates say the three local recovery centers opening Saturday — including Spanish-language-first service windows at each location — will help direct residents toward the aid they are owed. A FEMA spokesperson said applicants should not wait to gather complete documentation. 'Bring what you have,' she said. 'We can work with applicants to gather documentation over the course of the process.'

For one District 4 renter who gave only her first name, Maria, the FEMA news arrived as she was calculating how many more weeks her household could survive on a $400 church voucher she received in October. 'If this money comes through,' she said, 'maybe I can stop thinking about leaving.' She said she planned to be at the center on Martin Luther King Drive when it opens Saturday morning.

item.title: Eight weeks after Rafael, Rosa Elizondo is still drying out
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: A home health aide without a car rode out the storm with her three kids near the bay. Her rental still leaks, and she is still waiting for help to reach her block.
item.content:encoded:
There is a bucket in Rosa Elizondo's hallway. It has been there since September.

"When it rains, it fills. When it doesn't rain, it still drips a little, for fun," said Elizondo, 38, laughing in the way people laugh when the other option is crying. "My landlord says soon. Everybody says soon. Soon is my least favorite word in English. In Spanish too."

Elizondo, a home health aide and a mother of three, rents a duplex a few blocks from the bay in one of the low-income neighborhoods hit hardest by Hurricane Rafael. She has no car. She registered for a county evacuation ride before the storm, but when the time came she and her children rode out Rafael at home. The water stopped a few inches below her door. Homes a block closer to the bay flooded.

After the storm, people in neighborhoods like hers waited days for help; on some blocks, the first food and water came from church and neighborhood hubs, not official distribution. Elizondo got her first water and rice from the fellowship hall run by Pastor Gloria Whitfield a few blocks away.

Eight weeks later, the emergency has become a grind. Her back bedroom smells of mildew, and she moved her youngest, who is 6, into her own room. She still rides two buses to reach her clients, older people who need help bathing, eating and taking medicine. Some of them, she said, are in worse shape than she is.

"I take care of people for a living. Who takes care of the people who take care of people?" she said. "Not a complaint. A question."

Health officials said last month that emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay were still running about 40% above normal, long after they settled elsewhere in the county.

Whitfield said Elizondo's story is the story of half her list. "Everybody on my street is waiting on something: a landlord, an adjuster, a ride, a phone call back," she said. "People keep asking me about federal aid. I tell them I'll know when you know, and I'll knock on your door the same day." The state asked FEMA in October to add aid for households after damage assessments were slowed; no decision has been announced.

Elizondo said she does not need a lot. "A roof that stays a roof," she said. "And for somebody to tell me where to sign up before I hear it from my neighbor's cousin."

item.title: A second device, a longer wait: what Friday's find means for the Fort Hood brigade
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The Navy rendered a second explosive device safe near the channel entrance. A brigade's helicopters and equipment, already delayed twice, wait on the full sweep.
item.content:encoded:
When the Navy announced Friday that its teams had found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe, the news landed in two places at once: on the docks at the port, and about 230 miles north at Fort Hood.

One of the post's aviation brigades had been due to send its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer, bound for an overseas rotation. Hurricane Rafael pushed the movement back in September, and the Oct. 28 explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties delayed it again.

"We knew the search would take what it takes," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Our soldiers and families have been patient through a hurricane and now this. The brigade is ready. When the port is ready, we go." He declined to discuss the brigade's schedule, staging or destination beyond describing the mission as an overseas rotation.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, said no one was injured Friday and the search continues. She would not describe the device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been working the channel with the Coast Guard since the Navy said Oct. 30 that the Oct. 28 blast was caused by an explosive device.

Military logisticians plan around tides, cranes and berths. They do not plan around a closed channel with no reopening date. A second find means the Coast Guard is unlikely to reopen until teams are confident they have covered every stretch of water ships will use, and the Navy has said it will not put a date on that.

Locally, the military picture has been improving. Corpus Christi Army Depot returned to full production last week with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. But the depot fixes helicopters; it does not move them overseas. That still depends on the channel.

For families of soldiers in the brigade, the uncertainty is familiar. Price said the Army would announce the movement through public channels once it begins. "Nobody's going to hear it from a rumor first if we can help it," he said.

item.title: Bays closed by oil, pass closed by a blast: an Aransas Pass shrimper runs out of water
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Rafael. Seven weeks later, the bays are still closed to fishing and the pass to the Gulf is shut too.
item.content:encoded:
Every morning, Huy Nguyen walks the deck of his shrimp boat at the Aransas Pass harbor the way his father did. He checks the lines, the engine, the nets. Then he goes home, because there is nowhere to take the boat.

"Bays closed for oil. Pass closed for the bomb," said Nguyen, 51. "Where do I go? You tell me where, I go tomorrow."

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Sept. 18, days after oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal spread across about 33 square miles of water and shoreline in Rafael's surge. The closure was extended in early October. Cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, but the closure remains in place.

Hours earlier that day, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel at the entrance. The Navy has said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. For boats based at Aransas Pass, that entrance is the way out to the Gulf.

Nguyen started the season with what he called a fair run, squeezed by diesel prices. He keeps a spiral notebook of every trip, catch and fuel bill. The pages since mid-September are mostly blank.

"I write the date and I write 'no trip,'" he said. "My father would think I am lazy. I am not lazy. The water is closed."

He still owes on the boat and on the fuel dock, and he has a deckhand with two kids. He said he has not looked for other work yet because he does not know how long the closures will last. "If they tell me three months, I find something. If they tell me next week, I wait. Nobody tells me anything."

The bay shrimp season in Texas runs into late fall, so for families like Nguyen's, each week of closure is a week of the year's income gone. Shrimpers in the area say they want two things: a date, and a way to be made whole for the season they lost.

"Oil, I understand. A storm, I understand," Nguyen said. "This other thing, I don't understand. I just want to fish."

item.title: Why clearing a ship channel takes time, and what it means for a brigade that is still waiting
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Navy teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel after last week's blast. Officials won't put a date on reopening, and a Fort Hood brigade's equipment is waiting on it.
item.content:encoded:
From the seawall at Port Aransas, the work looks slow. Small boats move back and forth across the mouth of the channel, stop, and move again. That pace is the point.

Since the Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused the Oct. 28 blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay, Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating the explosion itself.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, would not describe the methods or equipment in use, citing safety and the ongoing investigation. "Our teams will search every yard of that channel they need to," Moreau said. "We are not going to rush it, and we are not going to put a date on it. When we say it is clear, we want it to be clear."

Clearing a channel is not the same as finding one object. Teams have to be confident that nothing else is there before the Coast Guard can let deep-draft ships back through. In a channel that carries tankers, cargo ships and military equipment, the cost of being wrong is measured in lives as well as dollars.

That caution has consequences up the road at Fort Hood. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment were supposed to pass through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer on the way to an overseas rotation. The movement was postponed in September as Hurricane Rafael closed in, and delayed again after last week's blast.

"Our soldiers and their equipment are ready to go," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "We'll move when the port is ready, and not before." Price declined to discuss timelines or where the brigade's equipment is staged.

For military families on the Coastal Bend and at Fort Hood, the delay is another stretch of not knowing. For the port, which has served as a strategic military seaport for decades, it is another week with its gate closed and its cranes idle. Officials say the search will set the schedule, not the other way around.

item.title: Found: the source of the GPS interference. Still unknown: who put it there, and why.
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The FBI says a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal was behind the interference pilots reported this month. Here's what that tells us, and what it doesn't.
item.content:encoded:
When pilots began reporting GPS interference near Corpus Christi this month, the first question was where it was coming from. On Sunday, the FBI answered part of it.

Investigators traced the interference to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said. "The investigation is ongoing," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division. "We won't be discussing what was found beyond that."
