What it tells us: The interference pilots reported within about 40 miles of the city came from a source on the ground. As Coastline Public Radio explained last week, satellite navigation signals are faint by the time they reach Earth, and a stronger signal on the same frequencies can drown them out for receivers in range. A transmitter in one spot can affect aircraft many miles away. That is also why the FAA described the problem by radius rather than by address: from the cockpit, interference looks like a zone, not a point on a map.

The FAA issued a notice to pilots Oct. 23, and relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters over ten days, kept landing using backup navigation. The FAA said Thursday that interference reports had stopped. "Pilots did exactly what they're trained to do," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "They reported it, and they flew safely."

What it doesn't tell us: who placed the vehicle there, how long it sat, why, and whether anyone has been detained. The FBI has not said, and Coastline Public Radio will not guess. Neither has the FBI said what kind of vehicle it was or exactly where it was parked.

For the relief effort, the practical story is already over: the flights landed, and the interference has stopped. For investigators, it is still unfolding, and Ellery made clear the FBI will set the pace of what becomes public. For pilots, Carver said, the lesson is the one their training already teaches: trust the backup, and report what you see.

Coastline Public Radio will report what the FBI releases, when it releases it.

item.title: Why the ER numbers still run high by the bay
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Countywide, emergency visits are back near normal, but low-income neighborhoods near the bay are running about 40% above normal. Health officials are still looking for the reasons, and residents describe what recovery looks like from there.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo knows which bus gets to the nearest hospital, where to transfer and how long the wait can be. Most of her neighbors know too. "Mira, in my neighborhood that's just general knowledge," she said. "Like knowing where the good tacos are."

Six weeks after Hurricane Rafael, emergency room visits across the county are back near normal, health officials said Friday. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where Elizondo, 38, rents and raises three children, visits are still running about 40% above normal.

"Averages can hide a lot," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The county looks close to recovered on paper, but these neighborhoods aren't there yet. We're working through the data to understand what's driving the difference, and we'll share what we learn."

The health district has not yet offered an explanation. But the map is familiar. These are the neighborhoods where, before the storm, advocates warned that many households lacked cars. At the storm's peak, about 2,900 calls a day poured into 911, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Afterward, residents there described waiting days for help, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution arrived.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs one of those hubs from her church's fellowship hall, was careful not to speak for the health district. "I can't tell you what the data means," she said. "I can tell you what I see. Folks without a car, without a regular doctor, and the ER is the only door that's open at 2 in the morning."

Elizondo, a home health aide, said she tells her clients not to wait when something is wrong. "Then I watch my own neighbors wait until it's an emergency, because getting anywhere is a whole production," she said. "Two buses, a transfer, somebody to watch the kids."

Shah said the health district's advice is the same everywhere: don't ignore chest pain, trouble breathing or a worsening wound, and call a doctor or nurse line when unsure. "We want people to get care," she said. "We also want to understand why some neighborhoods need so much more of it right now."

item.title: KNCB news director tells county commissioners that Spanish-language boil-water delay put lives at risk
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Marisol Fuentes-Vega, news director of KNCB Coastal Bend Radio, testified before the Nueces County Commissioners Court Friday that a 12-hour gap between the English and Spanish versions of the Sept. 26 boil-water notice represented a systemic failure in emergency communications equity — and called on the county to mandate simultaneous multilingual alerts.
item.content:encoded:
The news director of KNCB Coastal Bend Radio testified before the Nueces County Commissioners Court on Friday that the 12-hour delay between the English-language and Spanish-language versions of the Sept. 26 boil-water notice for Corpus Christi's Districts 3 and 4 constituted a systemic failure in the county's emergency communications system — one she said put the health of tens of thousands of Spanish-speaking residents at risk during the most critical period of the water contamination event.

Marisol Fuentes-Vega, who has led KNCB's bilingual newsroom since 2019, told commissioners that her station began receiving calls from confused Spanish-speaking listeners within hours of the English boil-water notice being issued. The official Spanish-language notice did not reach the station until 6:03 the next morning, she testified, 12 hours and 33 minutes after the English alert, and KNCB could not put an official notice on the air that it had not been sent. "For twelve hours our hosts were telling callers we had nothing official in Spanish," Fuentes-Vega told the court. "The question for this commission is: why were we in that position at all?"

The testimony drew on data KNCB compiled during the 30-day boil-water period, including call logs documenting listener confusion during the first day, interviews with community health workers in the Oak Park and Hillcrest neighborhoods, and an analysis of social media activity showing that Spanish-language shares of the boil-water notice lagged English-language shares by more than ten hours. Fuentes-Vega noted that the Texas DSHS preliminary investigation found 94.3 percent of gastroenteritis cases geocoding to the boil-water zone — neighborhoods where, she said, a large proportion of residents are Spanish-speaking.

Commissioners heard testimony from the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, which said the delay was attributable to reduced staffing at its translation contractor and acknowledged it would evaluate its procedures. Commissioner Isabel Noriega, whose precinct includes portions of Districts 3 and 4, called the delay "unacceptable" and introduced a motion directing the Office of Emergency Management to issue a new request for proposals for language access services that requires every life-safety alert to be released in other languages within 30 minutes of the English text. The motion passed 4–1.

Fuentes-Vega said after the hearing that the vote was a beginning, not a resolution. "We need a protocol with teeth — one that says the Spanish alert goes out the same minute as the English one, every time, with no exceptions," she said. "The storm is gone. The gap in our system is not." She said KNCB plans to continue covering the equity dimensions of Rafael's aftermath and would monitor the county's implementation of the new protocol.

item.title: The storm, photographed 6.2 million times: Rafael aerial archive opens to the public
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: FEMA has finished its aerial survey of the Corpus Christi area and posted reduced-resolution imagery from the first two phases. Here is what is in it and who can use it.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to see what Hurricane Rafael did to your block, you can now look for yourself. FEMA Region 6 said Friday that it has finished its aerial assessment of the storm and, starting the same day, made part of the imagery public.

The program ran from a baseline flown on Sept. 12, two days before landfall, through Oct. 29. In that time federal, state and contracted aircraft produced more than 6.2 million georeferenced image tiles covering 183 square kilometers of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area. FEMA called it the most comprehensive post-storm aerial survey conducted on the Texas Gulf Coast, and said the archive spans every phase of the disaster, from before the storm through the recovery still under way.

What is public is narrower than that. FEMA said downsampled imagery, meaning pictures at reduced resolution, from the Phase 1 and Phase 2 surveys is available through the agency's OpenData portal to academic researchers, local governments and community organizations working on recovery planning. Phase 1 was the residential and coastal survey behind the agency's first estimate, on Sept. 18, of 4,200 to 5,800 structures with major or severe damage. Phase 2, released Sept. 29, covered utility sites. Anyone who needs full-resolution imagery has to ask FEMA Region 6's geospatial office.

"This imagery archive is a resource that will support not just today's recovery, but future preparedness for the entire Texas Gulf Coast," FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said. He thanked NOAA, the Texas Army National Guard and the agency's contractors for flying the missions.

For neighborhood groups, the before-and-after pairing is the useful part. A baseline image from Sept. 12 next to one from the week after landfall shows which roofs, fences and trees were there before the storm, something that is hard to prove from memory. Tenant advocates and church relief hubs that have spent six weeks helping people document losses can now point to a dated federal photograph.

There are limits. Reduced resolution blurs the detail that matters most in a dispute over a single house, and an aerial picture still cannot see water damage under an intact roof. And the archive records what happened; it does not explain it. It is a record of the damage, open to more people than before.

item.title: What the jetty blast means for the Fort Hood deployment
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the Port of Corpus Christi has now been delayed twice, first by Hurricane Rafael and now by the channel closure. Here's how military port movements work, and why the channel matters.
item.content:encoded:
When the Army sends an aviation brigade overseas, most of its hardware doesn't fly there. It sails. Helicopters are prepared for the voyage, vehicles and containers are staged at a port, and a ship carries the load across the ocean while soldiers follow by air.

For a Fort Hood aviation brigade, that port is Corpus Christi, and the move has now been stopped twice. The brigade was scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer for an overseas rotation. That movement was postponed in September, when the Coast Guard put the port on storm footing ahead of Hurricane Rafael. On Friday, the Army said the move has been delayed again by the channel closure that followed Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

"Our soldiers and families have been flexible through two delays now," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Readiness doesn't stop because a schedule moves. We'll be ready when the port is ready."

Why Corpus Christi? The port is one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports, expected to handle military cargo alongside its commercial traffic. Its deep-water channel links Inner Harbor docks to the Gulf through a single entrance between the jetties at Port Aransas.

That single entrance is the point. Military port movements depend on a chain: rail or road from the post, staging at the port, a ship at the berth, and an open channel to sea. Break any link, and the movement waits.

The link that broke Thursday was the channel. Around 1 a.m., an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties, damaging the tug and injuring two crew members. The Coast Guard closed the channel to all traffic. Officials say the cause is unknown.

Fort Hood has not provided a new timeline, and this story does not speculate about one. Public affairs officers typically release movement details only when they are ready, and for good reason: schedules for military cargo are not something to publish in advance. When the Army is ready to announce a new date, Coastline Public Radio will report it.

item.title: Spill cleanup shifts to monitoring as a new emergency closes the channel
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Six weeks after the Inner Harbor spill, the Unified Command says cleanup is moving to a monitoring phase and inner-channel restrictions are lifted. The milestone arrived on the same day an explosion shut the ship channel.
item.content:encoded:
For six weeks, the Inner Harbor oil spill has set the rhythm of the Corpus Christi waterfront: boom along the shorelines, crews in the marshes, a wildlife hotline, and restrictions on ships moving through the inner channel.

On Thursday, the Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said shoreline cleanup is moving to a monitoring phase, and lifted the inner-channel restrictions that had been in place for vessel decontamination.

"This is a milestone for the crews who've been out on the shoreline since the winds dropped," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Monitoring means we keep checking the shorelines and the marshes, and we respond if oil turns up again. It doesn't mean we're walking away. If you see oiled wildlife, keep calling the hotline."

The spill began as Hurricane Rafael arrived, when the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, moored at the Rendal Terminals berth, released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude. Surge and wind spread sheen across about 33 square miles of bay, marsh and shoreline, reaching North Beach and Portland. Complaints of breathing trouble and skin irritation near oiled shorelines have since eased, health officials say.

For people who work the water, monitoring is not the same as reopening. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remain closed. "Reopening the bays to fishing is a separate decision, and it depends on testing," Whitaker said.

Huy Nguyen, a shrimper in Aransas Pass whose season was lost to the closure, took the news quietly. "Monitoring," he said. "OK. Monitoring doesn't put shrimp in the boat. Tell me when they test, and tell me what they find."

The milestone was overshadowed. Around 1 a.m. the same day, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties led the Coast Guard to close the ship channel to all vessel traffic. Two crew members were injured, and officials said the cause is unknown. With the channel shut, the newly lifted inner-channel restrictions changed little on the water Thursday, one more reminder of how much of this coast's recovery runs through a single channel.

item.title: On North Beach, the oil smell has faded. The questions haven't.
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Health officials say breathing and skin complaints near oiled shorelines have eased. A retired welder who smelled the oil arrive wants to see the proof for himself.
item.content:encoded:
Marcus Bell can tell you the day the oil smell reached North Beach. Two days after Hurricane Rafael, he said, he walked out his front door and it hit him "like a shop with the vents shut." He spent a career as a welder. He knows bad air.

"It's mostly gone now," said Bell, 67, standing on the sand a short walk from his house. "Mostly gone isn't gone. I'll believe it's clean when somebody shows me the numbers. I'm not saying it isn't clean. I'm saying show me."

In the first days after landfall, surge and wind carried oil from the Inner Harbor spill out of the ship channel and onto the North Beach and Portland shorelines and into marshes. Bell was among the residents cut off from downtown until the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened. Emergency rooms began seeing residents from near oiled shorelines with breathing complaints and skin irritation, and health officials advised avoiding contact with oil.

Those complaints have eased since early October, health officials say. "We've seen the shoreline complaints come down, which is what we hoped to see as cleanup progressed," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "Our advice hasn't changed. Avoid contact with oil, wash with soap and water if you touch it, and see a doctor if you have trouble breathing."

The cleanup itself continues. The Unified Command still restricts the inner ship channel for vessel decontamination, and fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remain closed.

For shoreline neighborhoods, the spill landed on top of the storm: flooded homes, closed bridges, and then a smell that kept windows shut for weeks. Residents like Bell say they want the same thing from the recovery now that they wanted in the first week, which is clear information delivered to the people living closest to the problem.

Bell has started walking the beach again some mornings, staying off the wet sand, and picks up what the tide leaves behind. "Shells, bottles, a flip-flop now and then," he said. "I said I'd wait for the official word, and I'm waiting. I'm just waiting closer. When the numbers come out, I'll check them against my own."

item.title: What GPS interference means for pilots, and why the relief flights kept landing
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The FAA has warned of GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi. Aviators train to fly without satellite navigation, and that training is being put to use.
item.content:encoded:
For most of us, GPS is the blue dot on a phone. For pilots, it is one of several ways to know exactly where the aircraft is. Near Corpus Christi this week, it is one they can't fully count on.

Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of the city, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice to aircraft operating in the area. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, part of an airlift of 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters that began Oct. 18, are continuing using backup navigation.

What is interference? GPS signals travel from satellites roughly 12,500 miles up, and by the time they reach Earth they are very faint. A stronger signal on the same frequencies, whatever its source, can drown them out for receivers in range. That is why interference reports are usually described by area rather than by a single point.

What do pilots do? "Every pilot is trained to navigate without GPS," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Ground-based navigation aids, air traffic control radar and onboard systems are all part of how flights continue safely when GPS isn't reliable. The notice makes sure crews know to expect it."

At the air station, Lt. Marcus Hale said aircrews flying into the field are briefed on the notice. "The relief flights are continuing," he said. "Crews are using backup navigation, which is exactly what they train for."

What we don't know: the source. Neither the FAA nor the Navy has said what is causing the interference or where it is coming from, and neither has said whether an investigation is under way. Officials generally do not discuss how interference is tracked down, and Coastline Public Radio is not going to speculate. The FAA's notice is written for aviation; we have asked the agency whether it has received reports from other users and will report what we learn.

For a base whose daily work is teaching student aviators to fly, the moment has an odd symmetry. The backup skills drilled into new pilots here are the same ones helping relief crews get supplies to the ground this week.

item.title: In Calallen, the neighborhood next to the water plant waits for the all-clear
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Leticia Ramos has organized her street's water runs for five weeks. With replacement pump parts finally at O.N. Stevens, she wants one thing from the city: a date.
item.content:encoded:
Leticia Ramos keeps a list. It names every household on her Calallen street: who has a car, who needs water dropped off, who has a baby or an aging parent at home. Since mid-September, it has been the backbone of her neighborhood's water runs.

"I'm a teacher. I make lists," said Ramos, 45. "Honestly, the list is the only thing that's run on schedule this whole time."

Ramos lives near the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant, which sits at Calallen on the Nueces River. When Hurricane Rafael cut both of the plant's power feeds early in the storm, pumps were damaged and water pressure dropped citywide. The city has been under a boil-water notice since Sept. 18. The plant has run on temporary pumps with limited capacity, and replacement parts, delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded, finally arrived Wednesday.

Ramos said she was glad to hear it, and frustrated by how she heard it. "We live next door to the plant and we find out what's happening from the TV," she said. "I don't need a promise. I need a date. And if the date changes, tell me why."

Teresa Gallegos, the water utility's spokesperson, said the utility won't set a date until the new parts are installed and testing is complete. "I understand the frustration, especially from the neighbors closest to the plant," she said. "The last thing anyone wants is for us to lift the notice and then have to put it back."

The notice applies to every household on the city's system, but Ramos' list shows how unevenly its weight falls. The households on her street that need water delivered are mostly older residents, people with disabilities and families stretching one car across two work schedules. Across the city, residents without cars, many of them in neighborhoods near the bay, have faced the steepest climb, hauling water by bus or on foot.

Ramos has already planned for the day the notice lifts. "Ice," she said. "Real ice, from the tray, in every glass on the street. We're going to have a block party, and the theme is tap water."

item.title: Forty flights in ten days: how the relief airlift into NAS Corpus Christi works
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Military C-17s and civilian charters are landing at a base best known for training Navy pilots. Here's why the air station, and why now.
item.content:encoded:
Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is a training base. On an ordinary weekday, the sky over Flour Bluff belongs to turboprop trainers flown by student aviators. Starting Monday, it also belongs to C-17s.

Over the next ten days, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charter flights are scheduled to land at the station with relief supplies, according to NAS Corpus Christi. The airlift is a visible new phase in the Coastal Bend's recovery from Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall on Mustang Island on Sept. 14.

Why an air station? A military airfield offers long runways, room to park and unload large cargo aircraft, and a secure place to stage freight before it moves on by truck. The C-17, the Air Force's workhorse cargo jet, can carry outsized loads into shorter runways than most airliners need, which is why it shows up after disasters.

"Our job is to give the relief effort a safe place to land and unload," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "The cargo belongs to the agencies doing the work in the community. We're the front porch."

Why now? The airlift comes as the region's sea route is only partly back. The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel last Thursday, with the inner channel still restricted for spill decontamination and ships queued at the offshore anchorage. On Sunday, the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded 40 containers, about a month after they were booked. Air and sea are now working the same problem from two directions.

The civilian charters operate under different rules than military aircraft, but Hale said all flights follow the same airfield procedures once they arrive. The station did not release daily flight schedules, which is standard practice at military airfields, and this story does not include them.

The airlift also marks another step back toward routine for the station itself. Its training aircraft flew to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm and began returning six days after landfall. For neighbors in Flour Bluff, the difference this week is in the sound: lower, heavier, and a lot more of it.

item.title: Four weeks into the boil-water notice, bay neighborhoods count the cost in jugs and bus rides
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Without cars, families near the bay haul water home on city buses. A church hub fills gaps, and neighbors say the wait for help has been longest where it is hardest to get around.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo has a system. Two gallon jugs ride on the bus seat beside her, a third sits between her feet, and at home a pot is usually on the stove, boiling. "Mira, I'm a home health aide," she said. "All day I make sure other people's water is safe. Then I come home and do it again for my own kids."

Elizondo, 38, rents in one of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay that took the worst of Hurricane Rafael's surge. She does not own a car. For nearly four weeks, since the city issued a citywide boil-water notice four days after landfall, her water routine has been built around bus schedules and a stove burner.

The notice followed the loss of both power feeds at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant, early in the storm. Pumps were damaged, temporary pumps have limited the plant's capacity, and the utility has said replacement parts were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded and parts had to ship from out of state.

The burden of that delay has not fallen evenly. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps leave many households near the bay without a way to get around. Since landfall, residents in these neighborhoods have described waiting days for help. Church and neighborhood hubs, which began handing out food and water before official distribution reached some streets, have become the closest supply many can reach on foot.

"If you have a car, a water line is an hour of your Saturday," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall. "If you don't, it's your whole day, and maybe your shift. I have elderly neighbors carrying cases of water up their front steps. That's not just a storm problem. That's a planning problem."

There is some good news. Health officials say emergency visits for stomach illness, which climbed sharply after the notice was issued, began easing weeks ago. Whitfield said the routine itself is what wears people down now: the hauling, the boiling, the math of how many jugs a family needs to get through a day.

Elizondo said she will believe the notice is over when the city says so, and not before. "Every morning my kids ask, 'Mami, can we drink from the sink yet?'" she said. "And every morning I tell them, 'Todavía no. Not yet.'"

item.title: Four weeks, 44,200 calls: the 911 center's long month, and what the record of it could show
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Call volume is nearly back to normal and borrowed dispatchers are going home. The center is keeping every call record for its after-action review.
item.content:encoded:
For 28 days the phones at the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center did not ring the way they are supposed to. On Tuesday they almost did. The center took 380 calls, it said Wednesday, close to the 310 it handled on an ordinary day before the storm.

Between those two numbers is the month that followed Hurricane Rafael. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the center handled more than 44,200 calls in the four weeks after landfall, about five times its normal volume. The peak came the day after the storm, at about 2,900 calls. The day after that brought a record 2,109 requests for rescue.

"Our dispatchers have shown extraordinary dedication over the past four weeks," Escamilla-Voss said. "The scale and duration of this response was unprecedented for our center, and I am incredibly proud of every person who answered calls, coordinated rescues, and kept working through the most demanding conditions I have seen in my career."

The center will begin returning to normal staffing over the next two weeks. The dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties who have worked alongside local staff since landfall will start scaling back on Thursday.

What stays is the record. Escamilla-Voss said the center is retaining all call records and audio as part of its standard after-action review. That archive is more than paperwork. Every call carries a time, a location and a type of emergency, and together they make a map of the storm drawn by the people who lived it: where the water rose first, where help was asked for most, and how long the asking went on.

It could also answer questions the center has not yet taken up in public. County officials said in September that the record surge in rescue requests came mainly from Districts 3 and 4. Those districts include some of the city's lowest-income neighborhoods, and they are the same ones that have been under a separate boil-water notice since Sept. 26. Whether callers there waited longer, or called more than once before help came, is something the records can show and a summary cannot.

The archive also holds the 23 calls from prepaid phones that sent responders to addresses where no one needed help, a cluster the center has referred to law enforcement.

Coastline Public Radio has requested the after-action review when it is complete.

item.title: Oil in the marsh, supper off the table: what scientists will watch as the bays recover
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: The bays stay closed to fishing more than three weeks after the spill. An oceanographer explains what recovery looks like, and a pastor explains what the closure means for families who fish to eat.
item.content:encoded:
At low tide, the edge of a Nueces Bay marsh tells the story in layers: green cordgrass on top, a dark band on the stems where the oil rode in on the surge, gray mud below.

"The marsh keeps a diary," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "That dark band is the entry for Sept. 14. Our job now is to read the next pages: how fast it fades, where it lingers, and what it does to the things that live there."

Oil from the Inner Harbor spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels released from two tankers as Hurricane Rafael closed in, spread across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Cleanup crews have worked the shorelines with boom since winds dropped, and the state opened a hotline for oiled wildlife. On Tuesday, Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in both bays; shellfish harvesting stays shut by order of the Texas Department of State Health Services.

Brooks said scientists will watch several things in the months ahead. Oil that settles into mud can break down slowly where oxygen is scarce. Marsh plants can recover if their roots survive. And shrimp, crabs and fish that grow up in the marshes are the link between the bay's health and people's kitchens. "Seafood testing is the bridge between the science and the dinner table," he said. "That's what will drive reopening."

He was careful about timelines. "Some places will look normal long before they are normal," Brooks said. "And some will look worse than they are. I'd rather say 'we'll know more after testing' than guess."

For some families near the bay, the closure isn't about sport. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the water, said many of her neighbors fish from piers and seawalls to stretch the grocery budget.

"You'd be surprised how many suppers in this neighborhood used to start with a bucket and a cast net," Whitfield said. "Now it's a can of something. People understand why. They don't want their babies eating oil. But it's one more thing that costs money they don't have."

She said the hall has added canned fish and beans to what it hands out. "If the bay can't feed us for a while, we'll feed each other," she said.

Brooks said he hopes long-term monitoring includes the places where people fish from shore. "The people on the seawall are the ones most likely to eat what they catch," he said. "They should be the first ones we're thinking about when we test."

item.title: State health investigators confirm waterborne contamination reached Districts 3 and 4 distribution lines
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Texas DSHS released preliminary findings Thursday showing 94.3 percent of confirmed gastroenteritis cases cluster inside the boil-water zone — and that the first ER admissions followed a documented pressure drop by exactly three days.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks after Corpus Christi issued a city-wide boil-water notice, state investigators have confirmed what neighborhood clinics and emergency physicians suspected: the pressure failure that swept through Districts 3 and 4 of the city's water distribution system in the days after Hurricane Rafael was not merely a supply inconvenience. It was a pathway for contamination that has made hundreds of people sick — more than 600 had been treated at the two main hospitals by Oct. 2, and the count is still rising.

The Texas Department of State Health Services released preliminary investigation findings Thursday afternoon. The analysis mapped every confirmed gastroenteritis case reported to Nueces County public health since Sept. 14 and found that 94.3 percent of them geocode to addresses inside the District 3 and District 4 service boundaries — the same geography covered by the boil-water notice. The concentration is what epidemiologists call a point-source distribution: cases spike sharply, then trail off, in a pattern consistent with a single contamination event in a shared infrastructure system rather than person-to-person spread.

"The epidemiological analysis shows 94.3 percent of confirmed cases geocode to the boil-water zone, and the temporal curve is consistent with distribution contamination rather than a community-wide respiratory or contact illness," the DSHS statement reads in part. The agency described its findings as preliminary, pending laboratory confirmation of additional stool samples and ongoing technical review of pressure records from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant.

The three-day lag finding is the most precise detail in the report. DSHS linked the onset of the pressure drop in the two districts — documented in distribution records — to the first wave of emergency room admissions for acute gastroenteritis in Districts 3 and 4. That 72-hour gap falls within the typical incubation window for the most common waterborne pathogens, and investigators said the temporal alignment strengthens their confidence in distribution contamination as the source.

Dr. Renata Obasi, an infectious disease specialist at a Corpus Christi hospital who reviewed the findings, described the zone concentration as "striking." "When you map these cases and they stack up inside a geographic boundary that corresponds exactly to a pressure event, you're not looking at coincidence," she said. "You're looking at infrastructure." She noted that pressure drops in distribution systems can allow contaminants to enter pipes through cracks and joints that remain sealed under normal operating pressure. The department said it is not in a position to identify the source of contamination pending further analysis and that the investigation into the pressure event itself remains open. The boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 — which covers approximately 48,000 residents — remains in effect.

item.title: In Flour Bluff, the night sky over the air station has gone quiet. The questions haven't.
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The drone sightings that stirred NAS Corpus Christi's neighbors after Rafael have stopped. The FBI's investigation continues, and officials still aren't saying what the lights were.
item.content:encoded:
On a clear night in Flour Bluff, the sky over NAS Corpus Christi looks mostly the way it did before the storm: navigation lights on training aircraft, a few bright planets, the slow drift of a satellite. Jaime Ortega still sets up his tripod in the backyard to watch.

"Most nights now, it's just the sky," said Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer whose videos of hovering lights over the air station circulated widely after Hurricane Rafael. "Which is what I wanted. I just wish I knew what I was looking at before."

The sightings came in a burst. In the days after the storm, residents began posting videos of lights hovering over the air station at night. NAS Corpus Christi said Sept. 20 that it was aware of drone reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations. The FBI's Houston division confirmed Sept. 23 that it was investigating. By late September, after about ten days, no new sightings were being reported.

Officials have not said what the lights were or who might have been flying them, and that may not change soon. The FBI does not discuss evidence in open investigations, and the Navy does not discuss how it protects its bases.

"Our position hasn't changed. We're still working with the appropriate authorities," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. "I'm not going to discuss security. What I can say is there was no impact to operations."

For neighbors, that leaves an unusual kind of uncertainty: a story that started loudly and then simply stopped. Some residents say they have stopped thinking about it. Others say they still glance up when they walk the dog.

Ortega has thought about what he would want if the investigation ever ends. "Not secrets. Not names," he said. "Just: here's what it was, here's what you can stop worrying about. That's all neighbors want."

He said he has kept every original file, with time stamps, in case investigators ever ask for them.

Meanwhile, the air station is getting busier. Training aircraft have been returning since Sept. 20, and for many neighbors, the sound of engines over Flour Bluff has become the reassuring kind of noise.

item.title: 'Built that way': KNCB's news director on why the Spanish water warning came 12 hours late
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: A state snapshot notes delays in Spanish-language alerts but puts no number on them. Marisol Fuentes-Vega has the number, and an explanation.
item.content:encoded:
Marisol Fuentes-Vega keeps the log open on her desk at KNCB. It shows the minute the station's fax line printed the city's boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4: 6:03 a.m. on Monday, Sept. 27. The English alert had gone out at 5:30 the evening before.

"Twelve hours and thirty-three minutes," said Fuentes-Vega, the station's news director. "I have read that line so many times I could say it in my sleep. For twelve hours, the people who listen to us were filling glasses from the tap."

On Tuesday the Texas Division of Emergency Management released its first after-action snapshot of public communications during Hurricane Rafael. The document notes "observed delays in Spanish-language alert distribution." It does not say how long the delays were, and it makes no recommendations.

The same day, a local chapter of the League of United Latin American Citizens filed a complaint with the state, citing its limited-English-proficiency plan and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. KNCB read the complaint on the air.

In an interview with Coastline Public Radio, Fuentes-Vega described what she says is a structural problem, not a one-night failure. English alerts, she said, move automatically from the agency that writes them to phones, television and radio. Spanish versions wait for a translation, and the translation waits for a person.

"Nobody decided that Spanish speakers should find out last," she said. "It is built that way. The English goes out at the speed of a computer. The Spanish goes out at the speed of whoever is still in the office."

KNCB is the main news source for an estimated 34,000 Spanish-speaking listeners in Corpus Christi. During the storm the station stayed on the air on generator power for as long as its transmitter held, translating warnings itself as they arrived.

Cassandra Trejo-Morales, a spokesperson for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, has said the Spanish notice was delayed and has attributed the delay to limits in the county's language-access service. The county has not yet said what it will change.

Fuentes-Vega said she is not waiting. The station now calls the city and the county every evening to ask whether anything has been issued in English that has not reached it in Spanish.

"It should not depend on us remembering to call," she said. "But until it doesn't, we call."

The state snapshot is a first look; a fuller review is expected later. Fuentes-Vega said she plans to ask county commissioners to require that every emergency notice go out in both languages at the same time.

item.title: Breathing complaints near oiled shorelines ease, but the bays stay closed
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Health officials say fewer people living near oiled shorelines are reporting respiratory problems. For North Beach and Portland residents, the relief is partial.
item.content:encoded:
On North Beach, Marcus Bell opened his windows this week for the first time in a while.

"Smell's mostly gone on my street. Not all the way. Mostly," said Bell, 67, a retired welder who has spent the weeks since Hurricane Rafael tearing out wet drywall. "My throat's better. I'll take it."

Health officials say Bell's experience fits a broader trend. Respiratory complaints from people living near oiled shorelines are easing, according to the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. In the first days after the spill, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from residents near the oil, and officials advised people to avoid contact with it.

"This is what we hoped to see," said Dr. Anita Shah, a district epidemiologist. "People are reporting fewer coughs, sore throats and headaches tied to the shoreline. That said, if you have asthma or COPD, or you're still having symptoms, see a doctor. And keep avoiding contact with any oil you find."

The bays themselves are not reopening yet. On Tuesday, Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, where the Texas Department of State Health Services has also closed shellfish harvesting. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across about 33 square miles of the bays after Rafael's surge and reached North Beach, Portland shorelines and marshes.

For shoreline neighborhoods, health and the bay are tied together. Many residents fish from piers and seawalls, some for sport and some for supper. For now, that food source is off the table. Shah said families who usually eat what they catch should not make an exception for fish that look or smell normal. "You can't see or smell everything that matters," she said.

Shah offered guidance for families near the shoreline. Don't touch oil or tar balls. If you get oil on your skin, wash it off with soap and water, not gasoline, kerosene or other solvents. Keep children and pets off oiled sand and out of the water. Don't eat fish or shellfish caught in the closed bays. And get care for persistent coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath or skin rashes.

Bell said he is ready for the next step. "When they say the beach is clean, I'll walk it," he said. "Until then, I've got walls to fix."

item.title: Two weeks after Rafael, neighborhoods near the bay say help came last
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay report waiting days for help after the storm. Many have no car, and church hubs filled the gap before official aid arrived.
item.content:encoded:
Rosa Elizondo remembers the days after Hurricane Rafael by what she ran out of. First ice. Then clean water. Then phone battery. Then patience.

"Nadie vino. Nobody came, not for days," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay. "I'm not saying nobody cared. I'm saying nobody came."

Two weeks after the storm, residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay are describing the same thing: they waited days for help after Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. Their accounts echo warnings made before the storm and patterns visible during it.

Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps left many households in these neighborhoods without a way out. When the mandatory evacuation came, residents without cars waited for county buses.

When the storm hit, the calls came from here. Calls to 911 peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

In the days that followed, churches and neighborhood hubs often reached these streets before official distribution did. "We had water and food on the table before anybody official was on this block," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall. "That's not a brag. That's a problem."

Whitfield said the reasons are not mysterious. "No car means you can't get to the site. No phone battery means you can't call. No English, sometimes, means you don't understand the recording," she said. "So you wait. And waiting looks like you're fine, when you're not."

Elizondo eventually got water from Whitfield's hall, a few blocks from home. What stung, she said, was the sense of being last in line. "In my job, I go to people's houses. I check on them. That's the job," she said. "I kept thinking, who's checking on us?"

How help reached different neighborhoods will matter for months as recovery continues. For now, Whitfield keeps her own list of who on her streets still needs what. "Somebody should be counting this," she said. "If nobody else will, I will."

item.title: In Aransas Pass, a shrimp boat that rode out the storm sits idle behind a closed bay
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Hurricane Rafael. His season may not survive the spill closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.
item.content:encoded:
The shrimp boat is tied up where it has been since the bays closed, lines doubled, outriggers folded, nets hung to dry along the dock rail in Aransas Pass. Huy Nguyen walks its deck every morning anyway.

"Habit," said Nguyen, 51. "My father did it every morning for thirty years. Now me. The boat doesn't know it's not going anywhere."

Nguyen's boat came through Hurricane Rafael with little more than scraped paint, a stroke of luck he does not take lightly. What it can't do is fish. Since Sept. 18, fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays has been closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife, and shellfish harvesting by the Texas Department of State Health Services, after oil from the Inner Harbor spill spread across about 33 square miles of water. Those bays are where Nguyen works.

The week of the storm, he found oil on his nets. "I knew then," he said. "You see that on your net, you know the season is gone."

Bay shrimpers had called it a fair start to the season this summer, with fuel costs eating into margins. Nguyen does the math out loud, the way he does most things. "I owe on the boat. I owe the fuel dock. I have a deckhand with two kids," he said. "Shrimp in the water don't pay the bank."

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. His family is part of the Vietnamese American fishing community that has worked the Texas Coastal Bend for decades, building a living one boat at a time. For many of those families, one lost season means a hard year.

The closures are meant to protect people from eating seafood that could be contaminated, and neither agency has said when they will be lifted. The cause of the spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal, remains under investigation.

Nguyen said he understands why the bays are closed. "I don't want anybody sick from my shrimp," he said. "But somebody needs to tell us how long. You can't plan a year on 'we'll see.'"

He has no plans to sell the boat. Not yet. "My father brought this boat through worse," he said, then reconsidered. "Maybe not worse. Different."

At the end of the dock, a pelican sat on a piling, waiting for a catch that wasn't coming in.

item.title: Spanish Boil Water Warning Came 12 Hours Too Late — Families in Districts 3 and 4 Drank Unboiled Water Overnight
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Spanish-speaking households in the boil water zone did not receive an authorized Spanish-language version of Sunday's emergency notice until Monday morning, leaving tens of thousands of residents without critical safety information for more than twelve hours.
item.content:encoded:
When the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority issued its boil water notice for Districts 3 and 4 on the evening of September 26, the warning reached English-speaking residents within hours through wireless emergency alerts, television broadcasts, and social media posts. For tens of thousands of Spanish-speaking households in the same affected zone, the authorized Spanish-language version of that notice did not arrive until the morning of September 27 — more than twelve hours later.

KNCB Radio News Director Marisol Fuentes-Vega said her station did not receive the official Spanish-language boil water advisory until 6:03 a.m. CDT on September 27. "We fielded calls all evening from families who had not heard the warning," Fuentes-Vega told Coastline Public Radio on Monday morning. "They wanted to know: is this real? Should we be doing something? And we could not point them to any official source because there wasn't one yet in Spanish." KNCB could not put an official notice on the air that it had not been sent, the news director said, and an unofficial translation is not the same as an authorized government advisory.

The delay traces to how multilingual emergency communications are handled. Official notices go out first in English; translation into Spanish and other languages is done by a county contractor, Nueces County Language Access Services, in a second step. Nueces County Office of Emergency Management spokesperson Cassandra Trejo-Morales confirmed the delay Monday and attributed it to reduced staffing at the contractor. "We are reviewing what happened and what can be done differently," she said — a response that advocates say does not answer why a life-safety notice could wait overnight.

That answer has not satisfied families who say they spent hours uncertain about the safety of their tap water. Rosa Guerrero, a mother of three living in Calallen, said she did not learn about the boil water notice until her daughter saw a post on social media the next morning. "By then we had already made dinner, we had given the kids water," Guerrero said. "No one had called us. The television alert was in English. We didn't understand it." Her account echoes those of dozens of residents who have contacted community organizations and KNCB since the gap became public.

At least two neighborhood associations in Districts 3 and 4 have written to the county demanding an immediate review of its emergency language access protocols. The American Civil Liberties Union of Texas said it is monitoring the situation closely. The county has not indicated whether it will conduct a formal after-action review of the multilingual alert gap. The boil water notice remains in effect for all 48,000 residents of Districts 3 and 4 regardless of when they received it — but for the families who cooked, drank, and bathed in that water through Sunday night, the question of accountability is already taking shape.

item.title: 23 Calls, No Victims: Nueces County Dispatchers Flag Cluster of False Emergencies Near Utility Sites
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Public records obtained by Coastline Public Radio reveal a puzzling pattern of unfounded 911 calls from prepaid phones clustering near utility infrastructure in the days after Hurricane Rafael.
item.content:encoded:
Coastline Public Radio has learned from Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center dispatch records, obtained through a public records request, that 23 calls received since September 21 from unregistered prepaid phones reported emergencies at or near utility infrastructure in northwest and central Corpus Christi, at least eleven of them describing trapped residents — and that in every case, responding units found no victims and no scene consistent with the caller's description.

The calls, which span four days beginning one week after Rafael's landfall, describe a range of scenarios: gas leaks, collapsed structures, elderly residents trapped in flooded homes. First responders who arrived at the named addresses found no evidence of any emergency. In several instances, the addresses sit within a few hundred yards of two electrical substations operating under reduced capacity since the storm.

Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor confirmed that the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center is reviewing the pattern. "Any time we see a cluster of unfounded calls that share characteristics — same type of phone, similar locations — we flag that internally," Vasquez-Okafor said. "We've referred the information to our law enforcement partners for assessment." She declined to characterize the calls as deliberate interference or to identify which agencies are reviewing the data.

The dispatch records show that all 23 calls originated from prepaid mobile numbers that return no subscriber information through standard law enforcement lookups. The calls clustered around the two sites, a pattern that Vasquez-Okafor acknowledged was noted by her team. No suspects have been publicly identified, and no charges have been filed. A source familiar with the matter, not authorized to speak publicly, said at least one federal law enforcement agency has received a referral. Emergency management officials say utility systems have not been affected by any of the false calls, and normal emergency response protocols remain in effect.

item.title: How the city's sewers spotted norovirus before the ERs filled
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal shortly before stomach-illness visits jumped about 180% above normal. Here's how the surveillance works, and what it can and can't tell us.
item.content:encoded:
Every flush in Corpus Christi ends up in the same place: one of the city's wastewater treatment plants. Samples from that water go to a lab. And on Monday, those samples told public health officials something the emergency rooms would confirm within days.

The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District announced that wastewater testing showed a norovirus signal and that stomach illness visits were rising. By Wednesday, ER visits for stomach illness were running about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use.

"People shed norovirus in very large amounts, often before they feel sick and sometimes without ever feeling sick," said Dr. Anita Shah, the district epidemiologist who runs the wastewater program. "So when it starts climbing in the sewer, that's an early warning. It tells us to get the hand-washing message out and to give the hospitals a heads-up."

How it works: Lab workers test samples for the genetic material of specific viruses. They track whether the amount is rising or falling over time. The results show a trend across the community, not a count of sick people.

What it can't do: Wastewater testing can't identify who is ill, which household or street the virus came from, or exactly how anyone was infected. "It's a trend line, not a diagnosis," Shah said. "It tells us the direction, and it tells us fast."

Why it matters after a storm: When the city's water plant lost power and pumps in Hurricane Rafael and the citywide boil-water notice followed, the conditions for stomach bugs to spread were in place: crowded homes, limited clean water for washing, long lines at distribution sites. Wastewater data lets officials see the spread across the whole city at once.

It also counts people who never see a doctor. Residents without a car, without insurance or without time off work are less likely to show up in clinic records. "Everybody uses the sewer," Shah said. "That makes it one of the fairest measures we have."

What to do now: Shah's advice hasn't changed. Boil tap water or use bottled water. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, because hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus. Stay home for two days after symptoms end. Get care for signs of dehydration.

The district will keep testing. "When the line starts to bend down," Shah said, "you'll hear it from us."

item.title: Lights over the air station: who investigates, and what residents should do
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The FBI says it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi. Here is how such reports are handled, why officials say so little, and how residents can help without getting in the way.
item.content:encoded:
For a week now, people in Flour Bluff have been watching the night sky over NAS Corpus Christi and posting what they see: small lights that hover, drift and disappear. On Thursday, the FBI confirmed it is investigating reports of drones near the air station.

That confirmation answered one question and raised several more. Here is what we know about how these reports are handled.

Who is responsible? Inside the fence, security is the Navy's job. The air station said Monday it is aware of the drone reports and is working with authorities, and that there is no impact to operations. The FBI can investigate potential federal crimes, including those involving drones near a military installation. The Federal Aviation Administration sets the rules for the airspace, and federal rules restrict drone flights over many military installations. Local police often take the first report from residents.

Why do officials say so little? "We can confirm we are investigating," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston division. "We have no further comment." That is standard. Investigators rarely discuss evidence, and the military does not talk about how it protects its bases. "We don't discuss security measures," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. "What I can tell people is that we're aware and we're working with the appropriate authorities."

Do the lights mean something is wrong? Officials have not said what the lights are. Hobby drones, aircraft lights, planets and satellites can all look strange at night, especially in phone videos. Jaime Ortega, a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos have circulated widely, has been careful to say only that he filmed lights he could not identify.

What should residents do? Write down the date, time, direction and duration. Keep original video files with time stamps. Report sightings to police rather than only posting them. Don't fly your own drone near the base, don't try to chase anything, and don't go onto base property.

What about rumors? Speculation spreads fast after a disaster. Sharing unverified claims about what the lights are, or about base activity, can confuse neighbors and make investigators' work harder.

What happens next? Investigations like this can take a long time, and the public may hear little until they end. For now, the air station's statement stands: aware, working with authorities, no impact to operations.

item.title: At the Army depot, hangars dry out while the workforce waits
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Corpus Christi Army Depot is working through hangar roof damage and water intrusion from Rafael. Its civilian employees are waiting for word on when to return.
item.content:encoded:
Training aircraft started coming home to NAS Corpus Christi this week, a visible sign that the air station is working its way back from Hurricane Rafael. A short drive across the station, at Corpus Christi Army Depot, the recovery is quieter and slower.

The depot, the Defense Department's primary facility for overhauling and repairing rotary-wing aircraft and their components, halted work before the storm and secured helicopters in its hangars. On Friday the depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and workers were told to stand by.

"Our people are the mission here," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "A lot of them are dealing with storm damage at home right now, and we want them focused on their families. We'll bring the workforce back as buildings are cleared and safe, and employees will hear it from their supervisors first."

Kowalczyk did not give a date for a return to work or describe which aircraft or components were in the affected hangars. The depot does not typically discuss specific aircraft in its work.

That restraint is normal, and so is the waiting. Roofs and the electrical systems beneath them have to be inspected before people and expensive equipment go back in, and water-damaged buildings need to dry out before anyone can judge what is salvageable.

For the Coastal Bend, the depot is also a paycheck. Its civilian mechanics, machinists and support staff live across the region, and the depot was hiring helicopter mechanics as recently as this summer. Every week on standby is a week of uncertainty for those households, even when the pay continues.

At NAS Corpus Christi, the return of aircraft from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth began Monday. "Getting aircraft home is the first step," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the air station's public affairs officer. He did not discuss schedules or numbers, which the Navy does not release.

For depot employees, the guidance for now is unchanged: stand by, watch for word from supervisors, and take care of home. Kowalczyk said the depot will share more as assessments are completed. "When there's news, our workforce hears it first," she said. "Then we'll tell everyone else."

item.title: FEMA Opens Spanish-Language Information Line for Rafael Survivors — Eight Days After Landfall
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Federal disaster information is now available in Spanish for Corpus Christi storm survivors, but advocates say an eight-day lag has already cost vulnerable families critical days of access.
item.content:encoded:
Eight days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall along the Coastal Bend, federal disaster information has become available in Spanish. Beginning today, callers who dial 1-800-621-3362 and press option 2 will reach a Spanish-speaking specialist on FEMA's Hurricane Rafael information line — a service that community advocates have been demanding since the morning the storm cleared.

FEMA Region 6 external affairs officer Rachel Ostrander said the agency has deployed bilingual Community Relations teams to shelters across Nueces and Aransas counties, and that translated information materials are now available in both print and digital formats. "We want every survivor to be able to get information in their language," Ostrander said. "Our teams are going to be on the ground, going shelter to shelter." FEMA Community Relations staff will conduct daily outreach rounds beginning tomorrow at the Richard M. Borchard Regional Fairgrounds, the Solomon P. Ortiz Community Center, and the Flour Bluff ISD gymnasium.

But for many in the Spanish-speaking community, the announcement arrives too late to undo a week of confusion. Corpus Christi is roughly 40 percent Spanish-dominant, and community advocates say that for eight days, monolingual families were navigating FEMA's telephone line and website without meaningful language support. Alicia Moreno, an organizer with the Coastal Bend Colonia Alliance, said her phone had not stopped ringing. "They couldn't get through. They didn't know what to click. Some of them gave up," she said. "Eight days is not a small thing when you're trying to find out what to do about a house that has no roof."

The delay reflects a recurring pattern in federal disaster response, one that equity advocates have flagged after hurricanes Harvey, Maria, and Ida. FEMA's disaster phone lines typically launch first in English, with Spanish and other language options added as capacity scales up. The agency does not publish a target timeline for Spanish activation. Critics say that gap — however the agency characterizes it — strikes hardest at the populations with the fewest alternative resources and the greatest unmet need. Moreno said her organization has been collecting the names of families who gave up on the English-only line and plans to work with FEMA's Community Relations staff to reach them before any household aid program opens.

item.title: Most of Rafael's rescues came by boat. Many of the boats belonged to the neighbors
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The Coast Guard's final count credits surface craft with 1,041 of 1,427 rescues. Eighty-seven of the people at the helm were civilians.
item.content:encoded:
The pictures people will remember from Hurricane Rafael are of helicopters: an orange-and-white Jayhawk holding steady over a roof in Flour Bluff, a rescue swimmer going down the wire. The numbers the Coast Guard filed Tuesday tell a somewhat different story. Most of the people who were rescued left by boat.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said it has submitted its formal summary of the search and rescue operation to Coast Guard District 8. The report certifies 1,427 rescues: 341 by helicopter hoist, 1,041 by surface vessel and 45 ambulatory survivor contacts. The surface count includes Coast Guard, state and civilian craft.

The civilians were not an afterthought. When officials announced the end of mass rescue operations on Sunday, they said 87 credentialed civilian boat operators had worked alongside 34 coordinated teams from the Coast Guard, Texas Task Force 1, the Corpus Christi Fire Department and the Nueces County Sheriff's search and rescue unit.

Credentialed is the important word. In the military and in the Coast Guard, an operation works because everyone in it is known to whoever is running it: who they are, what they are driving, where they have been sent. A volunteer in a bay boat becomes useful to a rescue the moment a dispatcher can give that boat an address and hear back what was found. Without that, the boat is one more thing in the water to keep track of.

The same idea shows up in a line of the report about drones. Contracted unmanned aircraft operators provided 112 thermal imaging annotations that were used directly to coordinate surface rescues, the Coast Guard said. A camera in the air found a warm shape on a roof or in the water; someone marked it; a boat went to the mark.

The helicopters did what only helicopters can do. In the first day and a half, when the wind was still blowing up to 55 knots and the water in the bayside neighborhoods was too rough and too full of debris for small boats, aircrews made 180 hoists and aircraft accounted for all 341 of the rescues by air that the final report certifies. The boats took over as the water calmed and the search moved inland.

The Coast Guard said a formal after-action review will be conducted within 90 days. For military families at the air station who watched crews fly around the clock last week, and for the neighbors who launched from flooded streets, that review is where the lesson of the two numbers, 341 and 1,041, gets written down.

item.title: A week after the spill, North Beach lives with the smell, and some with the cough
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Oil carried by Rafael's surge still marks shorelines and marshes. Health officials say residents near oiled areas should avoid contact with it and get care for breathing or skin problems.
item.content:encoded:
The first thing Marcus Bell notices when he steps outside his North Beach house in the morning is the smell. It is fainter than it was in the first days after the storm, he says, but it is still there, sharp and oily, when the wind comes off the water.

"I welded my whole working life around fuel and fumes," said Bell, 67. "I know that smell. You don't forget it."

A week ago, Hurricane Rafael's surge and wind carried oil out of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen spread across about 33 square miles of water, and oil came ashore on North Beach, on Portland's shoreline and in marshes along the bays. The Unified Command has estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, at the Rendal Terminals berth on the Inner Harbor.

For North Beach, the spill landed on top of everything else. When the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed as Rafael hit, residents like Bell were cut off from downtown until inspections finished and the bridges reopened Friday.

Since then, emergency rooms have seen respiratory and skin complaints from people living near oiled shorelines, according to the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District.

"If you live near the shoreline and you have a cough, a scratchy throat, headaches or a rash, you are not imagining it, and you should get checked," said Dr. Anita Shah, a district epidemiologist. "Most of those symptoms ease once people avoid exposure. The most important thing is to stay out of the oil and keep children and pets away from it."

Shah said residents who get oil on their skin should wash it off with soap and water, not solvents, and should not try to clean up oiled areas themselves.

Bell has mostly stayed inside with the windows shut. "My throat's been raw for days," he said. "I'm not going to the beach. Nobody's going to the beach."

Cleanup crews began deploying boom once winds dropped, and the state has opened a wildlife hotline for oiled birds and animals. Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services have closed fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

For Bell, the questions are simpler. "When does it go away," he said, "and who pays for my neighbors' doctor bills?"

item.title: In Calallen, next door to the water plant, neighbors run their own water routes
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Leticia Ramos lives near the O.N. Stevens plant that supplies the whole city. Under a boil-water notice, she has turned her street's group chat into a delivery network.
item.content:encoded:
Leticia Ramos keeps a clipboard on the dashboard of her SUV: names, addresses, how many people live in each house, who has a baby, who can't lift a case of water. By Sunday morning the list ran two pages.

Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher, lives in Calallen, a short drive from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the only plant that treats water for Corpus Christi. The plant lost both of its power feeds early in Hurricane Rafael on Tuesday, its pumps were damaged, and on Saturday the city issued a citywide boil-water notice.

"We live right next to the plant, and we've got less water than anybody," Ramos said. "I don't need another update that says crews are working diligently. I need to know when, and nobody will tell me when."

On Saturday, Ramos waited in line at a city water distribution site for more than an hour, then made three more trips for neighbors who are elderly, sick or don't have a car. By Sunday she had organized a rotation through her street's group chat: Whoever has gas and a free morning takes the list. The first run left at 7 a.m.

Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility, said she understood the frustration. "People who live near the plant see it every day, and they deserve straight answers," Gallegos said. "The straight answer is that we will lift the notice when testing shows the water is safe. Until then, please boil it, and please use the distribution sites."

Health officials say the best protection under the notice is to bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes, or use bottled water, for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and mixing baby formula. Hand-washing remains one of the most important things people can do.

The notice covers every tap in the city, from the low-lying neighborhoods near the bay where most 911 calls came from during the storm to the homes around the plant itself. For people without cars, a distribution site across town might as well be across the state, Ramos said. That is who her list is for.

"Teachers know how to run a list," Ramos said, tucking the clipboard back onto the dash before her next run. "This week, this is my class."

item.title: A machine counted the damaged houses. What the first Rafael survey can tell us, and what it can't
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: FEMA's estimate of 4,200 to 5,800 badly damaged structures comes from software reading drone photos. The range is wide for a reason.
item.content:encoded:
From a few hundred feet up, a house that lost its roof and a house that kept it are easy to tell apart. A house that kept its roof and took four feet of water is not. That difference sits inside the number FEMA released Saturday, and it is worth understanding before the number hardens into fact.

FEMA Region 6 said between 4,200 and 5,800 structures in Nueces County sustained major or severe damage from Hurricane Rafael. The estimate is based on what the agency called the first systematic aerial drone survey of the Corpus Christi metropolitan area: eight unmanned aircraft, operated under contract by Argus Aerial Systems, covering 180 square kilometers of residential and coastal zones on Friday and Saturday. The count was produced by automated analysis of about 847,000 image tiles.

Start with the range. A gap of 1,600 between the low and high figures is the survey being honest about itself. Software sorts each building into a damage class by what the camera sees: missing roof sections, collapsed walls, debris lines, standing water. Where the picture is ambiguous, the building can fall on either side of a line. FEMA called the figures preliminary and said they will be updated as the survey expands, including to the utility corridor and commercial districts.

Then consider what a camera pointed down cannot see. Surge damage happens low and inside: soaked drywall, ruined wiring, a failed foundation under an intact roof. The neighborhoods that flooded deepest are near the bay and the ship channel, and many of the homes there are older, smaller and rented. If water damage is undercounted anywhere, it is most likely to be undercounted there.

That matters because of how the numbers will be used. FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said the results are being shared with Nueces County emergency management and the City of Corpus Christi "to inform resource deployment." A map that shows heavy damage draws crews, tarps and inspectors. A map that shows less draws less.

None of this makes the survey wrong. It makes it a first pass. FEMA has said that whether households get direct federal help depends on joint damage assessments, and those involve people walking through homes. For residents, the practical advice is unchanged: photograph the damage inside as well as outside, especially the water line, before cleaning up.

item.title: Before official aid arrived, a church fellowship hall became a lifeline near the bay
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Church and neighborhood hubs are handing out food and water in low-lying neighborhoods that official distribution hasn't reached yet.
item.content:encoded:
The line outside the fellowship hall started before 8 a.m. Friday: a grandmother pulling a wagon, two teenagers carrying a cooler between them, a man in work boots who said he had come for water for his whole street.

Inside, Pastor Gloria Whitfield directed traffic from behind a folding table stacked with bread, canned beans, diapers and cases of water, some from the storage closet she stocked over the summer and the rest donated by church members and neighbors. Three days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, her hall in a low-lying neighborhood near the bay has become a pantry, a message board and, for some families, the only help they have seen.

Church and neighborhood hubs across the area are handing out food and water before official distribution reaches some neighborhoods, Coastline Public Radio found. In places where many households have no car, the hubs have one advantage no warehouse can match: People can walk to them.

"Nobody asked us to do this, and nobody needed to," Whitfield said. "These are our people. When you don't have a car, the nearest help is the help you can walk to. Right now, that's us."

Among those in line was Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who rode out the storm at home because she had no way to leave. She left with water, bread, a bag of rice and good news: Volunteers had checked on one of her elderly clients that morning. "She's OK. That's the best thing anybody's told me all week," Elizondo said. "Gracias a Dios, and thank you to the pastor."

The neighborhoods these hubs serve sit low and near the water. Emergency officials said most of the roughly 2,900 calls a day to 911 at the storm's peak came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates had warned before the storm that transit gaps leave many households there without a way to reach help.

Whitfield said donations were keeping pace for now, but she worried about water. Pressure has been low across the city since the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost power in the storm. "Water is the first thing people ask for," she said, "and it's the one thing I can't make."

She said she would keep the doors open until official help reaches her street, and after. "We'll be here when the trucks come," she said. "We'll be here when they leave."

item.title: Flour Bluff residents post videos of lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi at night
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: A hobby astronomer's clip of lights holding steady over the air station is circulating online. He says he doesn't know what they are, and he isn't guessing.
item.content:encoded:
Jaime Ortega pointed his camera at the sky Wednesday night for the same reason he always does. The storm had knocked out the city's lights, and for a stargazer in Flour Bluff, a dark sky is a rare gift.

Instead of stars, the 42-year-old hobby astronomer recorded something he could not identify: a few lights hovering over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, holding position, then sliding slowly sideways before blinking out.
