"I'm not saying what they are. I'm saying what I saw," Ortega said. "They weren't stars, and they didn't move like the airplanes I'm used to filming. In my log it says 'unknown,' and that's the honest word for it. I'd just like to know."

Ortega posted the clip Thursday. Other residents have posted their own videos of lights over the air station at night, and the posts have drawn a stream of theories in the comments, few of them grounded in anything.

For a neighborhood whose rhythms are set by the air station's training flights, the quiet since the aircraft left has been noticeable, and Ortega said that was part of why the lights caught his eye. "Normally there's always something moving over there," he said. "This week, nothing. Then these."

The air station sits at the south end of Corpus Christi Bay, beside Flour Bluff and the Laguna Madre. It is home to Navy flight training and to Corpus Christi Army Depot, the military's primary helicopter repair center. Its training aircraft were flown to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael made landfall early Tuesday, and the depot secured its helicopters in hangars.

NAS Corpus Christi did not immediately respond Thursday to questions about the videos.

Lights seen near an airfield at night can have many explanations, from aircraft seen at odd angles to reflections, and phone cameras often make distant lights look larger and stranger than they are. Military installations also generally do not discuss their security arrangements in public, so residents should not expect a detailed answer.

Ortega said he would keep filming on clear nights, noting the time and direction on every clip. "If it turns out to be nothing, I'll post that too," he said.

item.title: The helicopters came first to the bay. The boats are coming now to the Westside
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Two days after Rafael, searches are moving into neighborhoods where the water has not left, and where many people had no way to leave before it came.
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday evening the water on some streets in Molina was still above the knee, flat and brown and going nowhere. A woman on a porch there, who asked not to be named because she was worried about her landlord, had tied a yellow bath towel to the railing. She had heard on a neighbor's radio that it was what you were supposed to do.

It is. Nueces County Emergency Management said Thursday that residents who are still in their homes and need help should place a bright-colored item in a visible window or on the roof, and should not try to walk out through floodwater. The county said search teams had made 702 confirmed rescues as of 6 p.m., and that it had confirmed 23 storm-related deaths.

The first two days of this rescue belonged to the helicopters and to the neighborhoods on the bay. By Wednesday afternoon the Coast Guard had counted 341 people rescued by air, most of them from rooftops and upper windows in Flour Bluff and North Beach. Elena Vasquez-Okafor, dispatch chief of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, said Thursday that all known stranded survivors in Flour Bluff have now been reached.

What is left is slower. The county said operations have expanded into Districts 3 and 4, where surge flooding has persisted at depths of two to three feet in low-lying neighborhoods, and that Texas Task Force 1 swift-water units are conducting systematic grid searches in Greenwood and Molina. A grid search means every structure on every block, checked and marked, whether or not anyone called.

That matters in these neighborhoods more than most. Many households on the Westside do not have a car. Before the storm, county emergency managers urged people without transportation to sign up for evacuation rides, and advocates warned that the gaps in that system would leave people behind. People who could not leave are also less likely to have a charged phone two days after the power failed. A search that waits for a call will miss them. A search that goes door to door will not.

Shallow, standing water brings its own danger. It hides open drains and downed lines, and it is too shallow for a helicopter rescue to be the obvious answer and too deep for a child or an older person to walk through. The county's instruction is to stay put, signal and wait.

The woman with the towel said two boats had passed the end of her street before dark. She was going to leave the porch light off, she said, to save the battery in her flashlight, and listen.

item.title: Shoreline Regional at 140 percent capacity; second hospital full; state and federal medical teams requested
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Both major Corpus Christi area hospitals have reached or exceeded capacity two days after Hurricane Rafael, with storm surge trauma patients overwhelming emergency departments and officials requesting state and federal medical support.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — Shoreline Regional Medical Center has reached 140 percent of its licensed bed capacity as of Thursday afternoon, its chief medical officer confirmed, with the emergency department handling an ongoing wave of storm surge-related trauma injuries including drownings, lacerations, fractures, and crush injuries from structural collapse. Bay City Medical Center has also reported full capacity, with its emergency department temporarily diverting ambulance traffic to smaller outlying facilities.

Dr. Patricia Cabrera, Shoreline Regional's chief medical officer, described the situation as grave but controlled. "We are operating outside our normal parameters, and we are doing so safely," she said during a brief statement Thursday afternoon. "Our clinical staff is stretched, our supply logistics are under pressure, and we are managing. But we need additional clinical personnel and we need them now." The hospital has formally requested mutual aid support from the Texas Department of State Health Services and FEMA's National Disaster Medical System, citing the ongoing need for additional nursing and medical technician capacity in the emergency and intermediate care units.

The request was confirmed by the state health department, which said a medical support team was being mobilized and was expected to arrive within 24 to 36 hours. The team, which includes licensed medical personnel and mobile treatment equipment, will supplement hospital staff rather than establish a separate field clinic. Patients requiring specialized care beyond what local hospitals can provide are being transferred to facilities in San Antonio, with regional trauma centers there receiving Rafael patients as of Thursday.

Community clinics in the southern part of Corpus Christi and in the Calallen area have also been seeing increased walk-in traffic from residents with minor injuries or medication needs disrupted by the storm. The Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District urged residents with non-emergency medical needs to use those clinic locations rather than the hospital emergency departments. Residents who are on dialysis, insulin-dependent, or have other critical medication needs that were disrupted by storm evacuations were asked to call the county health hotline to arrange alternative supply coordination.

item.title: From space, Rafael's flood: About 43 square miles under water across three counties
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Radar satellites that see through clouds show where the surge went. A coastal scientist explains why the water reached where it did and why the low places matter.
item.content:encoded:
The images are gray and grainy and look nothing like a photograph. But the dark patches spreading across satellite radar imagery analyzed Wednesday tell the story of Hurricane Rafael's surge more plainly than any view from the ground: about 43 square miles of the Coastal Bend under water.

The flooding stretches across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island early Tuesday as a Category 3 storm and pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays.

"Radar is the right tool for a week like this, because it doesn't care about clouds," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "Smooth water bounces the radar signal away from the satellite, so it shows up dark. When you see dark where there should be streets and fields, that's flood."

Brooks compared the bays to a shallow baking pan. "Tilt a shallow pan and the water piles up at the low edge fast," he said. "Corpus Christi and Nueces bays are shallow. Eleven feet of surge doesn't just raise the water level. It shoves water into every low place along the shore, and it takes time to drain back out."

Those low places matter. Emergency officials said Wednesday that 911 calls peaked at about 2,900 a day during the storm, nearly ten times normal, and that most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Many are the same neighborhoods where advocates warned before the storm that transit gaps left households without cars to evacuate.

Coastline Public Radio plans to compare the flood footprint with census data on income and vehicle access, neighborhood by neighborhood, as more imagery becomes available.

Brooks said the same physics that moved the surge will shape where everything floating in the bays ends up as the water drains, from debris to the oil that spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived. The Unified Command estimates that release at about 9,000 barrels.

"I'd be careful about guessing where any of it has gone until people can get out and look," Brooks said. "Wind and water level decide that, and both are still changing."

Clouds have blocked ordinary satellite photographs since the storm's approach. Brooks said clearer images, and the first surveys from boats, should come as the weather breaks.

item.title: How do you map a flood you can't reach? Radar from a plane, then radar from space
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Two kinds of imagery, one from a hurricane hunter and one from satellites, are telling responders where Rafael's water went. Here is what each can and cannot show.
item.content:encoded:
On a radar image, calm floodwater looks like spilled ink. Streets, yards and parking lots that should scatter a signal back toward the sensor instead go dark, and the dark shape is the flood. That is the picture emergency managers have been working from since before sunrise Tuesday, when most of the places in it could not be reached by road.

The first image came from the air. The National Hurricane Center said a NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft made a final pass over the Corpus Christi area at about 3:30 a.m. Tuesday, roughly two and a half hours after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, and collected synthetic aperture radar imagery of Corpus Christi Bay and the ship channel. The center said the imagery shows the extent of surge flooding along the ship channel's industrial corridor and in coastal residential areas, and that it has been given to federal and state emergency managers, with copies going to FEMA Region 6 and the Texas General Land Office.

The second came from orbit. Satellite imagery analyzed Wednesday shows about 43 square miles flooded across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The two sources answer different questions. The aircraft pass is early and close: it covers the bay and the channel within hours of landfall. The satellite view is wide: it takes in all three counties at once.

What neither can do is count. Radar shows where water is standing at the moment the sensor passes over. It does not show how deep the water is inside a house, whether anyone is in that house, or what the wind did to the roof. The Texas Division of Emergency Management described the aircraft imagery as a first look before ground teams can safely enter, and as an input to initial damage estimates and to setting priorities for search and rescue. An input is not an answer.

It matters who is inside the dark shapes. Much of the low ground near the bay and along the channel is home to renters, older residents and households without a car, the same neighborhoods where county officials urged people before the storm to sign up for evacuation rides. A flood map tells responders where to look first. It will take people on the ground, going door to door, to learn who was there.

Officials have not released the radar imagery itself. They say more detailed surveys, flown lower and slower once the weather allows, will follow in the coming days.

item.title: Near the bay, a long night for neighbors who had no way out
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: In low-lying neighborhoods where many households don't have cars, some residents rode out Rafael at home. A pastor spent Tuesday trying to account for them.
item.content:encoded:
By late afternoon Tuesday, Pastor Gloria Whitfield had added two new columns to the penciled binder she keeps of neighbors without cars or working phones: people she had heard from since the storm, and people she hadn't. The second column was longer.

Whitfield, 59, coordinates relief out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-lying neighborhood near the bay, where many households don't own a car. She knows who they are, she said, because she is the one they call when they need a ride to a doctor's appointment or the pharmacy.

Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 storm and pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Power is out across much of the Coastal Bend. The city's water treatment plant lost both of its power feeds, and by morning, taps across Corpus Christi were sputtering.

Nueces County ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and sent buses for residents without cars. Advocates had pushed for months for more evacuation rides, warning that bus routes and transit gaps leave many households near the bay with few ways out.

"Some folks got on the bus. Some folks stayed because leaving meant leaving behind the little bit they've got, or because they've got a grandmother who can't be moved," Whitfield said. "I'm not judging anybody. I'm counting them."

With power out and many phones dying, Whitfield said, the only sure way to know who is safe is to go door to door, and she will not send anyone out until the wind lets up. "I told my deacons, nobody goes out in this," she said. "Tomorrow, we walk."

The neighborhoods she serves sit low and close to the water, and they are home to many of the city's households without a vehicle, a pattern transit advocates and emergency planners have flagged for years. In a storm, that combination means the people most exposed to the surge often have the fewest ways to get away from it, and the hardest time reaching help after it passes.

County officials have urged anyone who stayed behind to remain inside until conditions improve and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies.

Whitfield said the hall would need water, diapers and nonperishable food in the days ahead, but that for now her list was about people, not supplies. "First you find everybody," she said. "Then you feed everybody."

item.title: Seven times the calls, the same number of chairs: inside the first hours at the 911 center
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: The Coastal Bend's dispatch hub is at maximum surge capacity and borrowing dispatchers from two neighboring counties. What that means for someone waiting on the line.
item.content:encoded:
Somewhere in Corpus Christi this morning, a person is holding a phone and listening to it ring. The wind has dropped enough to hear the water moving in the street. The call will be answered, emergency officials say. The question on a morning like this is how long it takes, and who else is in line.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center, the 911 dispatch hub for Nueces County, said Tuesday morning that it is operating at maximum surge capacity as Hurricane Rafael moves inland. Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss said the center is receiving approximately seven times its normal call volume and has activated mutual aid with the dispatch centers in San Patricio and Bee counties.

"Our dispatchers are working alongside mutual aid partners to answer every call as quickly as possible," Escamilla-Voss said. "Please call 911 only for immediate life-safety emergencies. We need to keep the lines open for people in immediate danger."

Mutual aid is the system's pressure valve. A 911 center is built for an ordinary day, with a fixed number of consoles and people trained to work them. When calls multiply, neighboring centers take the overflow, answering as if they were in the same room and passing each emergency to the units that can reach it. It adds hands. It does not add boats, helicopters or passable roads, and during the height of a hurricane crews cannot always be sent, however fast the phone is answered.

That is why officials are asking people to sort their own calls. The center urged residents to shelter in place if it is safe to do so and not to call 911 for flooding updates that do not involve a person in immediate danger. People with non-emergency needs were asked to wait until the storm has passed and to check the City of Corpus Christi website and social media for road closures, shelters and power outages.

The burden of that advice does not fall evenly. A household with a car, a charged phone and a second floor can wait for information. A household in a one-story rental near the bay, with water coming in, cannot. The center has not said where today's calls are coming from. After past storms on this coast, the heaviest need has come from low-lying neighborhoods where fewer people had a way to leave.

If you must call: say where you are first, then how many people are with you and whether anyone is hurt. If the water is rising, move to the highest floor you can reach.

item.title: Rafael makes landfall with 125-mph winds; forecast put 9 to 12 feet of surge into Corpus Christi Bay
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: A reconnaissance pass over Hurricane Rafael after landfall confirmed a Category 3 storm with a well-defined eyewall and the most dangerous storm surge forecast the region has seen in decades.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — In what forecasters are calling the most dangerous Gulf storm to threaten the Coastal Bend in a generation, Hurricane Rafael made landfall near Mustang Island about 1 a.m. Tuesday with maximum sustained winds of 125 miles per hour. A reconnaissance aircraft pass over the storm about two and a half hours after landfall confirmed the eyewall was clearly visible on radar and that Rafael had maintained its Category 3 intensity through the final hours of its approach.

The reconnaissance data, transmitted in real time to the National Hurricane Center in Miami, showed a compact, well-organized storm with a relatively small eye — a configuration that forecasters had warned could mean more intense winds concentrated over a narrow swath near the center. The NHC's pre-landfall advisory placed the storm's surge potential at 9 to 12 feet for Corpus Christi Bay, with isolated areas possibly exceeding that range near the mouth of the ship channel and along Nueces Bay. "A storm surge of this magnitude would inundate virtually the entire barrier island and push several feet of water into low-lying mainland areas of the city," said a spokesperson for the NHC's storm surge unit in a final recorded advisory briefing aired on coastal radio stations.

Coastline Public Radio's Priya Raman, reporting from the station's inland backup studio north of the city, said the approach of Rafael felt qualitatively different from previous close calls the Coastal Bend had experienced. "People who stayed evacuated, people who thought about staying heard that surge forecast and left," Raman said. "Twelve feet is not an abstraction. That is the roof of a single-story home." She noted that emergency managers had been unambiguous in their public warnings that rescue operations would not be possible during the surge period.

The National Weather Service Corpus Christi office, also operating from a hardened backup location, issued a final set of local statements urging anyone still in a surge zone to move immediately to the highest floor of the strongest available structure. The eye of Rafael crossed Mustang Island in the pre-dawn darkness, with the most dangerous conditions — surge, extreme winds, and embedded tornadoes — expected to persist for three to four hours around and after landfall. Power outages were expected to be widespread and long-lasting across all of Nueces, San Patricio, and Aransas counties.

item.title: Empty flight lines and locked hangars: the bases wait out Rafael
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: With training aircraft in Fort Worth and depot helicopters secured in hangars, NAS Corpus Christi and the Army depot are buttoned up for the storm. Military families in surge zones fall under the same county evacuation order as their neighbors.
item.content:encoded:
From the Flour Bluff side of the fence on Monday, NAS Corpus Christi looked like a different place. No engines on the run-up pads. No trainers in the pattern. Just wind in the sea oats along the road and gray clouds stacking up over the Laguna Madre.

The air station and Corpus Christi Army Depot are buttoned up for Hurricane Rafael, which forecasters say will make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge. The Coastal Bend has been under a hurricane warning since Sunday afternoon.

NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday. The depot halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars the same day.

"Our aircraft are safe in Fort Worth, and our focus now is our people," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "After the storm, we'll assess the station and bring the aircraft home when it's safe to do that."

At the depot, Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist, said the workforce had done its part. "The hangars are locked down and our folks are with their families," she said. "That's exactly where we want them tonight."

Bases plan for storms the way they plan for everything else: by deciding in advance what moves, what stays and who does what. Aircraft that can fly leave. Aircraft in maintenance are secured indoors. Shops are emptied of anything that can blow or float away. The Navy does not discuss how many aircraft were moved or which personnel remain on station during a storm, and Coastline does not report those details.

The storm has also paused a larger military move. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement through the Port of Corpus Christi was postponed Saturday, as the Coast Guard put the port on storm footing. "Nothing's changed on our end," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "When the port is ready, we'll be ready."

For military families, the guidance is the same as for every other household. Those living in storm surge zones fall under the county's mandatory evacuation order. The county has opened shelters inland and is sending buses for residents without cars. Navy families should keep their information current in the Navy's family accountability system so commands can confirm they are safe after the storm.

By midafternoon, the first gusts were rattling the fence line. The flight line stayed empty.

item.title: The evacuation order came. For neighbors without cars, the wait began
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, residents without cars are waiting for county buses, and a church fellowship hall has become a place to charge phones, drink water and make calls.
item.content:encoded:
Pastor Gloria Whitfield kept Sunday service to one hymn and one prayer. Then she unfolded the table, opened the binder and plugged a power strip into the wall so neighbors could charge their phones while they waited.

County officials have made evacuation mandatory in the surge zones as Hurricane Rafael nears. Inland shelters are open, and county buses are making pickups for residents who do not have cars. In the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where Whitfield's church sits, that last part is the one that matters most. Here, leaving is not a decision. It is a wait.

"I have a man on my list who can't do the bus steps without help. I have a grandmother with four grandbabies and one suitcase. I have a lady who won't go anywhere without her oxygen and her cat, in that order," said Whitfield, 59. "Every one of them did what they were told. They called. They packed. Now they're waiting."

Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in these neighborhoods, a problem advocates raised all summer as they pushed for more evacuation rides. County emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for help in advance, and many did. On Sunday, the registrations turned into a line.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said buses were working through requests. "We are getting to people as fast as we can," he said. "If you're waiting, stay where we can find you."

Waiting has a cost that does not show up on a map. Families with cars left on Saturday or early Sunday, on their own schedule. Families without them are packing children, medicines and pets into a few bags and watching the street. Every hour of waiting is an hour closer to the weather.

On Whitfield's street, the driveways that were full Friday were mostly empty by Sunday afternoon. Inside the fellowship hall, a few neighbors sat in folding chairs with their bags at their feet, phones charging on the table, a television on the wall showing the forecast.

Whitfield moved down her list, calling each name, asking the same questions: Are you ready? Is your phone on? Did they call you back?

Asked when she would leave herself, she did not look up from the binder. "I'll go when my list is done," she said.

item.title: Fort Hood brigade's move through Corpus Christi postponed as Coast Guard sets storm condition
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The Army aviation brigade had been scheduled to ship its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer. A Fort Hood spokesman says the unit will be ready when the port is.
item.content:encoded:
On a gray Saturday afternoon, the cargo docks at the Port of Corpus Christi were quiet. The ship channel beyond them was nearly empty. And a move that the Army had planned for months was on hold.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement through Corpus Christi has been postponed as Hurricane Rafael approaches, officials said Saturday, the day the Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray, warning that gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation.

"Our soldiers are ready to deploy when the port is ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood. "The safety of the port, this community and our people comes first. We'll adjust the timeline and keep moving."

Price declined to give a new timeline or to describe where the brigade's equipment is now, consistent with the Army's practice of not detailing unit movements in advance. He described the destination only as an overseas rotation.

As Coastline explained last month, a brigade's port movement is a chain: equipment travels from the home post toward the seaport, is staged and prepared on the docks, and is loaded onto a sealift ship. A postponement means re-sequencing that chain, including ship schedules, staging space and the timing of soldiers' travel. None of that can be finalized until the storm passes and the port is ready to receive the ship.

The Port of Corpus Christi is a designated strategic seaport, sharing its channel between military cargo and one of the busiest crude export operations in the country. The port itself stayed open Saturday, though ocean-going ships had to arrange to leave or win Coast Guard approval to stay, and crude loading was tapering off.

The postponement comes a day after NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth and Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work to secure helicopters in its hangars. Together, the moves amount to a pause in much of the region's military aviation activity until the storm passes.

For military families, the immediate question is the storm, not the deployment. Price said Fort Hood would share updates on the brigade's movement when it could. Coastline Public Radio will report them when they are released.

item.title: Navy flies training aircraft from Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth; Army depot secures helicopters
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are moving training aircraft out of Rafael's path, and Corpus Christi Army Depot has halted work to secure helicopters in its hangars.
item.content:encoded:
The engines started early in Flour Bluff on Friday. Neighbors used to the rhythm of training flights noticed the difference: aircraft climbing out and turning north, one after another, and not coming back around.

NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael, Navy officials said Friday. Corpus Christi Army Depot, which sits on the air station, has halted work and is securing helicopters in its hangars.

"Moving the aircraft is a precaution. It's what we plan and train for every season," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "Our people and our aircraft will be out of harm's way, and we'll bring them home as soon as it's safe."

The reasoning is straightforward. Aircraft parked in the open are vulnerable to high winds and flying debris, and hangar space on any base is limited. Flying them inland, to a base well outside the storm's reach, protects them and lets training resume faster once the coast is clear. Navy air stations in Texas flew aircraft inland ahead of Hurricane Harvey in 2017 for the same reason.

Navy officials did not say how many aircraft were moved or which units were involved. Coastline Public Radio does not report those details, or the movements of personnel, unless the Navy releases them.

At the depot, the Army's primary facility for overhauling and repairing helicopters, workers spent their last shifts before the storm securing aircraft and shops. Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot, said the workforce did the job and went home.

"Our workforce did what they always do. They secured the aircraft, they secured the shops, and now they're going home to take care of their families," Kowalczyk said. "We'll tell them when it's time to come back."

The forecast cone has covered Corpus Christi since Thursday, though no hurricane watch had been issued as of Friday morning. Hale said base residents and families should follow guidance from their commands and county emergency management.

For the neighborhoods around the air station, the quiet will be noticeable. Training flights are as much a part of daily life in Flour Bluff as the wind off the Laguna Madre. When they stop, people know something is coming.

item.title: Why a soaked Coastal Bend matters before Rafael's center ever arrives
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Tropical moisture and a stalled front have saturated soils and pushed the Nueces River up at Calallen. Here is how wet ground, a rising river and the bay can work together, and who lives closest to the risk.
item.content:encoded:
On a street near the bay Tuesday afternoon, a storm drain gurgled and gave up. Water spread across the gutter and into a front yard that had not dried out since the morning downpour. A boy in rain boots stood at the edge of it, deciding whether it was deep enough to be worth it.

Tropical moisture pumped north ahead of Tropical Storm Rafael ran into a stalled front and soaked the Coastal Bend on Tuesday. Soils across the region are saturated, and the Nueces River is rising at Calallen. Rafael itself has not yet reached the Gulf; forecasts show it crossing the Yucatan Peninsula on a west-northwest track toward Texas.

That combination matters before the storm's center gets anywhere close. When soil is dry, it absorbs a large share of the rain that falls on it. When it is saturated, almost all new rain runs off into streets, ditches and creeks, and from there into the river and the bays.

"Rain on saturated ground is like pouring water into a full glass," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "It doesn't matter how gently you pour. It's going over the side."

Hydrologists call the next part compound flooding. Rivers drain to the coast. If a storm then pushes seawater into the bays, the river water has fewer places to go, and low-lying land near the water can flood from two directions at once: rain and river from behind, surge from the front. Which way it plays out depends on the storm's track, strength and timing, none of which is known yet for Rafael.

The geography of that risk is not evenly shared. The neighborhoods nearest the bay include many of the region's lowest-income households, and bus service and transit gaps leave many of those households without cars. Advocates have pushed all summer for more evacuation rides. Wet weeks are a reminder of why: the people with the shortest distance to the water often have the longest path to leaving.

What to watch: the weather service posts readings for the Nueces River gauge at Calallen online throughout the day, along with river forecasts when they are issued. Track and intensity forecasts for Rafael will tighten over the coming days.

What to do: keep storm drains clear where it is safe, move cars out of low spots, avoid driving through water, and if you do not have a car, register for evacuation help through 2-1-1 now.

item.title: With a storm in the Caribbean, a church starts working its list
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield began calling neighbors without cars this weekend, days before anyone knows where Tropical Storm Rafael will go.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday afternoon, after the last service let out, Pastor Gloria Whitfield sat down at the folding table in her church's fellowship hall, opened the three-ring binder and started at the top of the list.

Whitfield, 59, keeps a penciled list of neighbors who have no car, no working phone, or both. Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Saturday, and early forecasts show it heading west-northwest across the Yucatan Peninsula, with Texas a possible target. Nobody knows yet whether it will come anywhere near Corpus Christi. Whitfield decided not to wait to find out.

"If it turns, wonderful," she said. "Then I had a nice visit on the phone with a lot of people I love."

Her questions are the same for every call. Do you have two weeks of medicine? Is there someone who can drive you if you have to leave? Have you called 2-1-1 to register for an evacuation ride? Is your phone charged, and do you have a way to charge it if the power goes out?

The calls are her answer to a problem advocates have raised all summer. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates have pushed for more evacuation rides. The county's answer has been the state's evacuation assistance registry: residents without cars are urged to sign up so planners know where to send buses.

The reason to start early is time. A household with a car can decide to leave in an afternoon. A household without one has to find out about a ride, get on a list, pack for children and pets and medicines, and be ready when a bus or a neighbor arrives. Every step takes longer, and every step depends on someone else.

One of the afternoon's calls went to Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who does not own a car. She laughed when she heard who it was. "Pastora, I know, I know," Elizondo said. "This week. For real this time."

Whitfield made a small mark next to the name and moved down the page. By early evening she had reached most of a column. She said she would finish the rest Monday, holiday or not.

"The storm doesn't know who has a car," she said. "But we do."

item.title: The pastor with the list: who has no car, who has no phone, who needs a hand
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Pastor Gloria Whitfield runs meals and supplies from her church fellowship hall near the bay. Before every hurricane season, she updates a list that no agency keeps.
item.content:encoded:
The list lives in a three-ring binder on a folding table in the fellowship hall, between the coffee urn and a stack of donated diapers. Pastor Gloria Whitfield keeps it in pencil. The list started years ago in a spiral notebook she carried in her purse; this summer she copied it into the binder.

"People move. People pass. People get a car and lose a car," said Whitfield, 59. "Pen is for people who think things stay the same."

The binder holds the names and addresses of neighbors who have no car, no working phone, or both. Some pages have notes in the margin: can't do stairs, needs oxygen, won't leave without the dog. Whitfield started it, she said, because nobody else in the neighborhood had one.

Her neighborhood sits near the bay, and it is the kind of place where her list is long. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates have pushed this summer for more evacuation rides for residents who cannot drive themselves out. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to register with the state's evacuation assistance registry by calling 2-1-1, so planners know where to send buses.

Whitfield supports the registry and helps people sign up, sometimes at that same folding table, on her own phone. She also knows what a registry cannot do. "A registry is a list in somebody's computer. Mine is a list with a face on it," she said. "I know which man can't climb the bus steps without help. I know which grandmother won't leave without her grandbabies' birth certificates and won't find them without me."

Relief agencies have spent the summer stocking warehouses ahead of peak hurricane season. Whitfield's warehouse is a storage closet behind the kitchen: cases of water, canned beans, baby formula, batteries. "When the big trucks come, they go to the big parking lots," she said. "We're the little parking lot. Somebody has to be."

What advocates describe as a transit gap is, in practice, a question of time. A family with a car can leave when the order comes. A family without one has to find a ride, wait for it and be ready when it arrives, often with children, medicines and pets. The longer that chain, the more likely someone is still at home when the weather turns.

Whitfield closed the binder and slid it back under the table. "Nobody should have to be brave because they're poor," she said. "That's the whole sermon."

item.title: How an Army aviation brigade gets from Central Texas to a ship in Corpus Christi
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer. Here is how a port movement like that generally works.
item.content:encoded:
On most mornings, the Port of Corpus Christi is about oil. Tankers ride low in the ship channel, and more wait offshore. But from time to time, the port's cargo docks fill with something else: rows of tan Army vehicles and helicopters with their rotor blades folded back, wrapped against the salt air and waiting for a ship.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation, Army officials have said. They have not released dates, and the Army typically does not describe unit movements in detail before they happen, for security reasons. This explainer describes how such movements generally work, not the specifics of this one.

A move like this starts at the home post. Units inventory and prepare their equipment, then send it toward the seaport by rail and by highway convoy. At the port, vehicles and aircraft are staged on the docks, inspected, cleaned and prepared for the voyage. Helicopters are typically readied for sea transport with blades folded or removed and protective wrapping applied, because salt spray is hard on aircraft.

Most of the equipment then rolls aboard a sealift ship, often a roll-on, roll-off vessel built to carry vehicles. Soldiers usually travel separately and meet their equipment at the other end.

The Port of Corpus Christi is one of a small number of commercial ports designated as strategic seaports, which means it commits to making berths and staging space available for military deployments. That role shares a single ship channel with one of the busiest crude export operations in the country, where tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage for a berth. Military movements are scheduled around that traffic.

Weather is a factor in any port movement, especially now. The Atlantic hurricane season peaks in September, and port operations of every kind can pause when the Coast Guard restricts the channel ahead of a storm.

For residents, the signs of a movement in general are easy to spot: military vehicles on the highways, convoys near the port and aircraft on the docks. Fort Hood's public affairs office is expected to share details when it decides they can be released, and Coastline Public Radio will report them then.

item.title: On the first day of school, a mother's bus commute shows the gaps on the map
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: For households without cars near the bay, the city bus is the plan for work, for school and, if it comes to that, for a hurricane. Advocates want more evacuation rides.
item.content:encoded:
The morning bus is running late, and Rosa Elizondo has already done the math. If it comes soon, she can walk her youngest to the school gate and still reach her first client on time. If it doesn't, she calls ahead and apologizes, the way she has many mornings before.

Elizondo, 38, is a home health aide and a mother of three. She rents in a low-income neighborhood near the bay and does not own a car. On Monday, the first day of school for her children, her commute looked the way it looks most days: a bus, a walk, another bus, a lot of waiting. "Mi carro es el bus," she said, laughing. "My car is the bus. And the bus has its own opinions."

Her situation is not unusual. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and community advocates have spent the summer pushing for more evacuation rides for exactly those residents. The neighborhoods with the fewest cars are often the ones closest to the water.

County emergency managers held hurricane preparedness fairs this summer and urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before a storm, so planners know where to send buses. In Texas, the list is the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, which residents can join by calling 2-1-1.

Elizondo said she still has the registration card from the county's preparedness fair but has not sent it in. "I sign up my clients. I'm always signing up somebody else," she said. "Me, I think, okay, the neighbors, the church, somebody will have a car."

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs meals and supplies from her church's fellowship hall in the same part of town, said that is the gap advocates worry about most. "Everybody is counting on somebody with a car, and the people with cars are the first ones to leave," Whitfield said. "We need rides that come to the people, not people who have to go find the ride."

Elizondo's two older children caught the school bus at the corner. She walked her youngest, who is 6, to the gate herself and waved until the door closed. Then she checked the bus schedule on her phone, frowned, and started walking toward the next stop.

item.title: Church pantries stock up for storm season in neighborhoods that know the gaps
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, church relief hubs are filling shelves now, because residents say help has to start close to home.
item.content:encoded:
The fellowship hall at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church is starting to look like a warehouse. Cases of bottled water line one wall. Canned beans, rice, diapers and baby wipes cover the folding tables. A whiteboard by the kitchen tracks what has come in and what is still needed.

"Batteries," Whitfield, 59, said, pointing at the board. "Everybody brings beans. Nobody brings batteries."

Relief agencies across the Coastal Bend are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders are signing standby relief contracts so larger shipments can move quickly. In neighborhoods near the bay, church and neighborhood hubs are doing their own version of the same work.

The reason is practical. Many households here do not have a car, and bus gaps already make it hard to reach a grocery store across town on an ordinary day, as Coastline Public Radio reported last month. Advocates say people without cars will turn first to places they can walk to.

The pattern is not unique to Corpus Christi. Disaster researchers have long noted that in neighborhoods with fewer cars and fewer resources, people tend to turn first to nearby institutions they already trust, such as churches, corner stores and community centers, especially in the first days after a disaster.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who relies on buses, stopped by on a recent evening with her kids to help sort donations. "They help me all year. This is me helping back," Elizondo said, as her youngest stacked cans into a crooked tower. "Also, the air conditioning in here is better than mine. Don't tell her I said that."

Whitfield said she is not trying to replace county or federal relief, only to cover the hours or days before it arrives. "When the big trucks come, praise God," she said. "Until then, it's us. It has always been us first."

Her notebook of neighbors without cars or phones has grown this summer, she said, and she has been helping people register for evacuation assistance through the state's 2-1-1 registry. She wants county officials to see hubs like hers as partners. "We already know who needs what," she said. "Use us."

item.title: Inside the depot's hiring push: why the Army's helicopter repair shop wants local mechanics
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Corpus Christi Army Depot is recruiting helicopter mechanics this summer. The work is exacting, the hangars are hot and the jobs tend to last.
item.content:encoded:
The short description of the work at Corpus Christi Army Depot is that it fixes helicopters. The long description takes a while.

The depot, on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, is the Defense Department's primary depot for rotary-wing aircraft maintenance. Army helicopters arrive worn from years of flying, and the depot's civilian workforce takes them apart, inspects and repairs airframes, rebuilds engines and components and sends the aircraft back to units. This summer, the depot is hiring helicopter mechanics to keep that work moving.

"These are careers, not gigs," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "People come in as mechanics and retire as mechanics, and in between they've touched aircraft that flew all over the world. There's a lot of pride in these hangars."

Kowalczyk said the depot looks for people with aviation maintenance training, military experience or industrial trade backgrounds, and it trains new hires on Army procedures and standards. The work is precise, documented and inspected at every step. "Everything gets checked, and then it gets checked again," she said. "That's the culture."

The hangars are also hot in August, and Kowalczyk did not pretend otherwise. "It's South Texas. Our folks hydrate, and they look out for each other," she said.

For the Coastal Bend, the depot's hiring matters beyond the base fence. Its civilian payroll ripples through Flour Bluff, the Southside and beyond, and the skills it builds, from sheet metal and hydraulics to wiring and avionics, are the kind that stay in a community.

The work also connects to readiness far from Texas. Helicopters rebuilt here go back into service with years of flying left in them, and the pace of that work affects how many aircraft Army units have available. That link is why depot hiring is about more than local jobs. For job seekers, it also means steady hours and federal benefits in a region where many skilled trades rise and fall with oil and construction.

The depot shares the air station with Navy flight training squadrons, which have flown a normal summer schedule, and with a Coast Guard air station. Openings are posted on USAJOBS, Kowalczyk said, and the depot encourages applicants who are new to aviation to apply if they have strong mechanical skills.

item.title: What a "show of force" exercise is, and why analysts pay attention
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: A foreign government's announced naval and special-operations drills have drawn attention far from where they will take place. Here is how to read them.
item.content:encoded:
When a foreign government announced large naval and special-operations exercises this week, analysts quickly reached for a familiar phrase: a show of force. For listeners in the Coastal Bend, where many families have someone in uniform, it is worth unpacking what that means, and what it does not.

Exercises are normal. Militaries train constantly, and big exercises are how they test whether ships, aircraft and units can work together under pressure. The U.S. military runs large exercises every year, often alongside allies.

Some exercises are meant to be seen. A "show of force" is an exercise whose audience is as much political as military. Announcing it publicly, holding it far from home and making it large are ways of telling other governments: we can operate here, at this scale. The drills announced this week were described as taking place far from the Gulf and involving both naval forces and special-operations units.

Special operations change the signal. Naval drills demonstrate reach. Adding special-operations forces, small units trained for raids, ship boardings and quiet work in contested places, suggests a government wants to show it can do more than sail ships in formation. That combination is one reason analysts are paying close attention.

What analysts watch next: the size of the forces actually involved compared with what was announced, whether the drills run longer than planned, how close they come to other countries' forces and what officials say while they are under way. An exercise that ends on schedule usually tells you one thing. One that keeps growing tells you another.

A note on language: officials and analysts often use "exercise," "drill" and "maneuvers" interchangeably. What matters more is scale, location and timing, which is why careful analysts wait for drills to begin before drawing conclusions.

Closer to home, the routine continues. Training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi have been flying a normal summer schedule, and the air station said late last month that base services were operating normally after a routine inspection.

As any veteran will tell you, early reports from far away are often incomplete. Coastline Public Radio will follow the exercises as more becomes public, and will stick to what can be confirmed.

item.title: In Aransas Pass, a second-generation shrimper reads the bay and the fuel gauge
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Huy Nguyen has worked the bays of the Coastal Bend most of his life. This summer's catch has been fair. The math has not.
item.content:encoded:
Huy Nguyen keeps two kinds of records. One is in his head: where the shrimp were running last week, how the water looked, which way the wind will turn by afternoon. The other is a stack of fuel receipts clipped to the visor of his truck.

"The first one tells me where to go," said Nguyen, 51, who owns a shrimp boat out of Aransas Pass. "The second one tells me if I can afford to go."

Bay shrimpers describe a fair start to the season, and Nguyen agrees. But fuel costs have squeezed margins for small operators all summer, and boats that look busy from the harbor are often working for very thin returns.

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. He learned the bays on his father's boat, and he still talks about the water the way his father taught him to: as something alive that changes by the hour. The shallow marshes and seagrass beds that ring the bays are nurseries for young shrimp, crabs and fish, and the health of those habitats shows up, eventually, in his nets.

Mornings at the Aransas Pass docks start in the dark. Deckhands load ice and check the nets and winches, and the boats file out past the harbor markers before the heat sets in. By afternoon they are back, sorting the catch on deck while buyers wait on the dock.

"People think of the bay like a parking lot full of shrimp," he said. "It's not. It's a nursery. You take care of the nursery, the shrimp come. You mess up the nursery, you can have all the cheap fuel in the world and it doesn't matter."

For coastal towns like Aransas Pass, the shrimp fleet is part economy and part identity. Family operations depend on the bays, the docks, the ice houses and the buyers who take the catch, and a bad stretch for one tends to ripple through the others.

Nguyen said he has no plans to stop. His crew is small, his boat is old but sound, and the bays have been good to him more years than not. "I'm not complaining," he said, then reconsidered. "OK, I'm complaining about diesel. Not the bay. Never the bay."

item.title: No car, no easy way out: bus gaps shape life, and storm plans, in neighborhoods near the bay
item.dc:creator: Priya Raman
item.description: Many households in Corpus Christi's low-income neighborhoods near the bay don't own a vehicle. Advocates say evacuation plans have to start with that fact.
item.content:encoded:
At 6:10 on a weekday morning, the bus shelter near Rosa Elizondo's rented duplex is already warm. She has made the trip so many times she can tell the time by the light on the bay: first bus, a transfer downtown, a second bus, then a walk to her first client's door.

"If I miss one bus, my whole day moves," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three. "If the bus is late, I'm late. If my kid is sick, I'm counting bus times in my head before I'm counting fevers."

For many households in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, life is organized around a bus schedule. Census data show these neighborhoods have some of the highest shares of households without a vehicle in the city, and service that works for a weekday commute can leave long gaps at night, on weekends and across town.

Advocates say those gaps matter most when the question is not how to get to work but how to get out. Nueces County emergency managers have been urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance at preparedness fairs this summer. Advocates want more: more pickup points, more rides and more outreach door to door.

"A plan that starts with 'get in your car' isn't a plan for my street," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall. "A lot of the people I feed on Wednesdays have never owned a car. They need a ride, and they need someone to knock on the door and tell them the ride is coming."

The county's registry is a start, Whitfield said, but it depends on people knowing about it, having a phone to call and trusting the system enough to use it. She has been sitting with neighbors to help them sign up.

Elizondo said she thinks about storms the way she thinks about buses: in terms of what happens if one thing goes wrong. "Everybody says, 'Just leave.' OK. In what?" she said, then laughed. "My neighbor's truck? The pastor's car? I'll take whatever's going. Pero somebody has to be going."

Coastline Public Radio is mapping transportation access across the Coastal Bend this hurricane season. If you live without a car and want to share how you would evacuate, contact our newsroom.

item.title: Fort Hood aviation brigade to ship helicopters through Port of Corpus Christi in late summer
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The brigade's helicopters and equipment will move through the port on the way to an overseas rotation, Army and port officials said Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
An Army aviation brigade from Fort Hood will move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer on the way to an overseas rotation, Army and port officials said Wednesday.

"Our soldiers are trained and ready, and our equipment will be too," said Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood. "We'll be ready to deploy when the port is ready for us, and the Port of Corpus Christi has been a reliable partner in getting Army equipment where it needs to go."

Price did not give a date or a destination beyond describing the movement as an overseas rotation, which is standard practice for unit movements.

Rotations like this one separate people from equipment. Soldiers typically fly. A brigade's helicopters, vehicles and containers travel by road and rail to a port, where they are inspected, staged and loaded aboard a sealift ship. Helicopters are usually prepared for the voyage with rotor blades folded or removed and protective wrapping against salt air.

Corpus Christi is a natural choice. The port is one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports, and it has handled Army deployments before.

For the port, a brigade movement is a familiar if infrequent job. Military equipment is handled at general cargo docks rather than at the crude terminals that dominate the channel, where tankers have been loading at a near-record pace this summer. Staging can take days, as equipment arrives, is checked against load plans and is positioned for loading.

"This is a community that's proud of its military connections, and the port is proud of this role," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We'll work the military cargo alongside our regular business. Our people know how to do both."

For residents, the most visible part of a brigade move is usually the staging at the docks rather than anything on the water. The Army has not released details of how or when equipment will arrive in Corpus Christi, and Coastline Public Radio does not report unit movement details before public affairs officials release them.

Families with questions about the rotation should get information through their soldier's unit and its family readiness group.

item.title: NAS Corpus Christi completes routine readiness inspection; base services normal
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: The air station says a scheduled inspection has wrapped up with no change to day-to-day services for service members, civilian workers or families.
item.content:encoded:
Naval Air Station Corpus Christi has completed a routine readiness inspection, and base services are operating normally, the station's public affairs office said Monday.

"This was a scheduled inspection, the kind every installation goes through, and it's complete," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "The gates, the clinic, the commissary and the flight line are all running normal hours. Families shouldn't notice anything different."

For people outside the military, the word "inspection" can sound like trouble. It usually is not. Installations and commands are inspected on a regular cycle to make sure equipment, facilities, training and emergency plans meet Navy standards, and the detailed results generally stay inside the chain of command. The station did not release results, which is typical.

Preparing for an inspection usually means weeks of extra work: checking maintenance logs, updating emergency plans, inventorying equipment and making sure training records are current. For the people who do that work, the end of an inspection mostly means getting back to the regular job.

The air station hosts Navy flight training squadrons, which have been flying a normal summer schedule, along with tenant commands that include Corpus Christi Army Depot and a Coast Guard air station. The depot has been hiring helicopter mechanics this summer.

For the Flour Bluff and Padre Island neighborhoods around the base, the practical meaning of Monday's announcement is that nothing changes. The morning training flights continue, the gates keep their usual hours and the people who work on the station keep their routines.

That routine is a big part of life on this end of the city. Base employees fill the lunch spots along the main roads into the station, and the training schedule sets the rhythm of the sky overhead.

For military families, the bigger summer news on base has been more ordinary: moving season, with new arrivals reporting in and others packing for their next assignment.

Hale said questions about base services can go to the station's public affairs office. Coastline Public Radio covers the Coastal Bend's military installations and the families connected to them.

item.title: Summer in the pattern: student pilots keep NAS Corpus Christi busy
item.dc:creator: Sam Delacroix
item.description: Training squadrons at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi are flying a normal summer schedule, and in Flour Bluff the sound of turboprops is part of the morning.
item.content:encoded:
On a weekday morning in Flour Bluff, the first sound after the mockingbirds is usually a propeller. Training aircraft from Naval Air Station Corpus Christi climb out over the water, turn, and come back around, again and again, as student naval aviators work the landing pattern.

Summer is not a slow season at the air station. Its training squadrons are flying a normal summer schedule, according to the station's public affairs office, moving students through a syllabus that eventually sends them on to advanced training and the fleet.

"Summer is a normal training season for us," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "Students are flying, instructors are flying, and the base is operating the way it's supposed to. If you live nearby, that's the sound you're hearing."

For listeners who do not work on base, it helps to know what shares that patch of land at the end of Ocean Drive, between Corpus Christi Bay and Oso Bay. NAS Corpus Christi is home to Navy flight training, and it hosts tenant commands that include Corpus Christi Army Depot, where civilian workers overhaul Army helicopters, and a Coast Guard air station. The depot is also hiring helicopter mechanics this summer.

Flight training works like a pipeline. Students arrive with classroom training behind them, learn to fly in the local pattern and over nearby outlying fields, and leave qualified for the next stage. The pace is steady by design, which is why the sound over Flour Bluff changes so little from week to week.

For anyone who has served, the rhythm is familiar. Training commands run on schedules built months in advance, and a normal summer schedule means the syllabus is moving as planned: students are progressing, aircraft are available and instructors are in the cockpit.

For the surrounding neighborhoods, the base is both a neighbor and an employer. Many families in Flour Bluff and on Padre Island include someone who works on the station, in uniform or as a civilian, and the morning traffic at the gates tracks the training day.

Hale said residents with questions about aircraft noise or base activity can contact the station's public affairs office. "We'd rather answer a question than have people guess," he said.
